label: Board assured of fairness review by Chief Officers
original_label: Board assured of fairness review by Chief Officers

label: Asset parking and warehousing transactions
original_label: Asset parking and warehousing transactions

label: Off-balance-sheet treatment euphemism
original_label: Off-balance-sheet treatment euphemism

label: Mischaracterizing proceeds as gifts
original_label: Mischaracterizing proceeds as gifts

label: Nuisance fee to disguise unauthorized payment
original_label: Nuisance fee to disguise unauthorized payment

label: Put option masks guaranteed payment to LJM
original_label: Put option masks guaranteed payment to LJM

label: Credit rating agencies and Wall Street deceived by structure
original_label: Credit rating agencies and Wall Street deceived by structure

label: Enron appeared more successful than it was
original_label: Enron appeared more successful than it was

label: LJM as independent third-party entity
original_label: LJM as independent third-party entity

context: The charging document recites the accounting rules that were supposed to protect against off-balance-sheet abuse, suggesting FASTOW relied on the existence of these rules and their purported compliance as a defense.

original_label: Transactions purportedly complied with accounting rules

original_label: Cuiaba project costs minimized in framing

label: Hedging transactions mask financial manipulation
original_label: Hedging transactions mask financial manipulation

label: Hedging against market risk reframed as stock protection
original_label: Hedging against market risk reframed as stock protection
quote: Talon, which was created in April 2000, was designed by FASTOW, GLISAN, and others to protect Enron's balance sheet from decreases in value of certain of these investments. label: LJM investment presented as independent third-party funding
original_label: LJM investment presented as independent third-party funding

label: Back-dated hedge transaction
original_label: Back-dated hedge transaction

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement

label: Nigerian barge financing dressed as third-party sale
original_label: Nigerian barge financing dressed as third-party sale

label: Undisclosed fee for asset transfer
original_label: Undisclosed fee for asset transfer

original_label: Parking and warehousing asset arrangements

original_label: Complex structures presented as sophisticated and clever

original_label: Stock price inflation presented as corporate benefit

original_label: Condor structures treated as legitimate because off-balance-sheet compliant

original_label: MCAS as extension of pre-existing function

original_label: AR concurrence with MCAS downplaying strategy

original_label: Dismissing repetitive MCAS activation as non-safety issue

original_label: Pilot error framing in post-crash response

original_label: Compliance determination despite system gaps

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties

original_label: Saving costs through reduced testing and analysis

original_label: Production schedule as reason for proceeding despite warnings

original_label: Schedule pressure as external constraint on management

One of the mantras that we had was the value of a day and making sure that we were being prudent with our time, that we were being thorough, but yet, that there was a schedule that needed to be met.

original_label: Cost and schedule as impracticality rationale

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance

original_label: Changed Product Rule compliance

original_label: Financial competitiveness driving re-engining decision

original_label: EICAS exception framed as cost-safety tradeoff

original_label: EICAS absence characterized as non-consequential

original_label: Revenue service entry pressure

original_label: Annunciator functionality absorbed into generic alert

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement

original_label: No single individual required to share test data

label: Pilot response time assumptions exceed guidance
original_label: Pilot response time assumptions exceed guidance

original_label: Boeing dismisses post-crash pilot training criticism

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance

original_label: Compliance sufficient despite human factors gaps

If Boeing had applied for a new type certificate for the 737 MAX 8, would it have made a difference to the level of scrutiny of the aircraft during certification? Would seeking certification via a new TC have produced a safer aircraft? The answer from the experts was consistent; each said a new TC would not have produced more rigorous scrutiny of the 737 MAX 8 and would not have produced a safer airplane.

original_label: Avoiding certification complexity to maintain commonality

original_label: Faulty AOA triggering characterized as scenario not reality

original_label: System design as compensating for AOA failures

original_label: Southwest contract penalty driving training decisions

original_label: Test pilot reaction framed as catastrophic scenario

context: The TAB's flight controls assessment frames the Lion Air and Ethiopian accidents as resulting from sensor failure rather than system architecture that made the system dependent on one sensor.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Design changes demonstrate compliance via procedures
original_label: Design changes demonstrate compliance via procedures
quote: The TAB has reviewed this change on the MAX and has determined that the current emergency procedures, coupled with the changes to MCAS, will be sufficient in mitigating MCAS anomalies related to automatic pitch trim.
context: The TAB's stabilizer trim cutout switches assessment uses procedural compliance to justify accepting a design different from earlier B737 NG models.

label: Pilot trim system deficiency attributed to training programs
original_label: Pilot trim system deficiency attributed to training programs
quote: Evidence presented in the preliminary JT610 and ET302 accident reports suggests deficiencies in both flightcrews' trim system understanding, awareness, and use. These deficiencies may not have been individual, but may have been due to their respective airline training programs.
context: The TAB's training evaluation attributes accident causation to airline training deficiencies rather than to system design or design communication.

label: Pilot trim competency assumptions prior to accidents
original_label: Pilot trim competency assumptions prior to accidents
quote: SSAs, such as those performed by Boeing for the MCAS, estimate the likelihood of a flightcrew's improper management of trim system anomalies. Prior to the two accidents, Boeing's estimate of this occurrence may have been reasonable, as judged from witnessing the events in simulation. However, after the two accidents, it appears that the estimate was optimistic.
context: The TAB acknowledges that Boeing's pre-accident assumptions about pilot trim management competency proved wrong, but frames this as an estimation problem rather than a design problem.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: 14 CFR compliance justifies design qualification
original_label: 14 CFR compliance justifies design qualification
quote: There is currently no FAA regulation or guidance that specifies maximum trim crank/hand wheel forces, other than the qualitative statement in 14 CFR 25.143 (b) that pilot actions for controllability and maneuverability shall not require exceptional piloting skill, alertness, or strength.
context: The TAB cites the absence of specific regulatory limits to frame high manual trim forces as meeting the regulatory standard.

label: Stabilizer runaway notes omission deemed manageable
original_label: Stabilizer runaway notes omission deemed manageable
quote: The QRH procedures for Stabilizer Trim Inoperative include notes stating that manual forces may be high and may require two pilots to operate the trim wheel, however the QRH procedures for Runaway Stabilizer do not include those same notes.
context: The TAB notes a procedural inconsistency without characterizing the consequences of missing information when pilots face a runaway stabilizer emergency.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Development assurance plan audit satisfies compliance
original_label: Development assurance plan audit satisfies compliance
quote: Action item closed. Audit completed. The TAB evaluated and accepted the Development Assurance Accomplishment Summary document.
context: The TAB's resolution of a systems engineering concern relies on completing a process audit rather than substantive technical finding.

label: B737 NG service history supports procedure adequacy
original_label: B737 NG service history supports procedure adequacy
quote: The TAB concluded that with the enhanced training package, pilots will be able to successfully complete the separate IAS DISAGREE and AOA DISAGREE NNCs. This was also validated in the JOEB activity and supported by B737NG service history.
context: The TAB minimizes concern about procedural ambiguity by invoking prior aircraft experience without addressing whether that experience applies to the novel AOA DISAGREE condition.

label: Design escapes framed as requirements and process issues
original_label: Design escapes framed as requirements and process issues
quote: Boeing and Collins Aerospace have had two design escapes that have not been analyzed for root cause. One was a design error for the Auto Stab Trim Monitor in the fault tree for the Low Altitude Stabilizer Runaway failure condition. The other was a requirements issue that resulted in the presence of an AOA Disagree message being tied to the AOA Indicator option on the primary flight display (PFD) instead of the monitor always being functional regardless of the AOA display option.
context: The TAB labels system failures as procedural rather than design problems, framing them in passive terminology.

label: Manual trim forces deemed acceptable after flight test data
original_label: Manual trim forces deemed acceptable after flight test data
quote: The manual trim wheel forces were not representative of the actual aircraft, so they were not evaluated. Boeing subsequently provided flight test data and analysis in Boeing Report, 737-8/-9 Stabilizer Trim Wheel Forces to show that the manual trim wheel forces were acceptable.
context: The TAB accepts Boeing's flight test data regarding high manual trim forces without independent verification or specification of the operational context in which those forces would be encountered.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Software compliance achieved through DO-178B processes
original_label: Software compliance achieved through DO-178B processes
quote: The processes used by Collins Aerospace are consistent with the expectations of DO-178B acceptable means of compliance. The artifacts reviewed provided a high level of confidence that the software implements the required behavior as documented in the system requirements allocated to software, and assurance that no additional unsafe functionality has been introduced.
context: The TAB's software assessment concludes safety adequacy by reference to process compliance with an industry standard.

label: Government relied on Boeing's self-selected compliance consultant
original_label: Government relied on Boeing's self-selected compliance consultant
quote: The Government now believes that Boeing can be trusted to select a compliance consultant because Boeing has made "meaningful progress in improving its anti-fraud compliance and ethics programs." In summary, the Government's position in this lawsuit has been that Boeing committed crimes sufficient to justify prosecution, failed to remedy its fraudulent behavior on its own during the DPA which justified a guilty plea and the imposition of an independent monitor, but now Boeing will remedy that dangerous culture by retaining a consultant of its own choosing.
context: The court critiques the Government's rationale for accepting the NPA's compliance provision, noting the Government's deflection from direct oversight to Boeing's self-selection of a monitor.

label: Consultant will work with Boeing to address FAA concerns
original_label: Consultant will work with Boeing to address FAA concerns
quote: When asked by the Court how the Boeing-selected consultant would stop a culture of fraud, the Government said that the independent consultant would work "next to Boeing" to make sure it is "reacting and appropriately addressing any concerns raised by the FAA." It then will "report to the government on what they are seeing" and if necessary, "make recommendations for improvements."
context: The court describes the Government's explanation of the consultant's role, which places responsibility for addressing fraud culture on Boeing's reactions rather than independent enforcement.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: NPA secures meaningful accountability and public benefits
original_label: NPA secures meaningful accountability and public benefits
quote: The Government declares that the NPA "secures meaningful accountability, delivers substantial and immediate public benefits, and brings finality to a difficult and complex case whose outcome would otherwise be uncertain." Specifically, it states the NPA requires Boeing pay the maximum statutory fine, further pay into a crash-victim compensation fund, and commits Boeing to compliance improvements.
context: The court summarizes the Government's stated justification for dismissing the criminal charge in favor of the NPA, framing the agreement as serving the public good through accountability and victim compensation.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Boeing agreed determination of DPA breach left to Government discretion
original_label: Boeing agreed determination of DPA breach left to Government discretion
quote: Neither is the Government's contention that Boeing may litigate whether it actually breached the DPA a serious justification because Boeing agreed that determination was left to the Government's sole discretion.
context: The court notes that the Government cited technical contractual language as a basis for confidence in the NPA, treating a procedural compliance matter as sufficient reassurance.

label: Government claims uncertainty and litigation risk of acquittal
original_label: Government claims uncertainty and litigation risk of acquittal
quote: The Court further agrees with Movants that the Government's claim of "uncertainty and litigation risk presented by proceeding to trial" is unserious. The Government has a confession from Boeing, signed by the CEO and Chief Legal Officer, admitting to all the elements of the conspiracy charge against it in the DPA. As such, the assertion that there is a legitimate risk that Boeing would be acquitted at a trial lacks support.
context: The court criticizes the Government's minimization of the strength of its case as a justification for dismissal, noting Boeing's confession undermines claims of trial risk.

label: Government downplays acquittal risk citing technical pilot jury verdict
original_label: Government downplays acquittal risk citing technical pilot jury verdict
quote: The Government asserts the risk of acquittal is legitimate because a jury acquitted a technical pilot of various charges related to his role in testing the 737 Max. This overlooks the nature of the charges made against the two Defendants. The technical pilot's central defense was that he was a scapegoat for the broader and systematic failure of Boeing's corporate culture which led to the crashes. The Government agrees with that theme, given the nature of the information filed in this case and the stipulated facts agreed to by Boeing, which targets the corporate culture.
context: The court notes the Government's use of a different acquittal to suggest trial risk, while acknowledging that the Government's own case targets corporate-level culpability, not individual technical responsibility.

label: NPA obligations unenforceable if statute of limitations has run
original_label: NPA obligations unenforceable if statute of limitations has run
quote: Movants contend that if the Court believes the Government's reasons are unsupported, it may hold that dismissal is clearly contrary to manifest public interest. Namely, Movants state that the dismissal is against public interest because: (1) the NPA is an "unprecedented effort to short-circuit Rule 48(a)'s judicial review requirement;" (2) Boeing's obligations are unenforceable under the NPA because the statute of limitations has run, meaning the Government would be unable to refile charges against Boeing even if it breached
context: Victims' families argue that the NPA structure displaces future accountability by making Boeing's obligations unenforceable due to statute of limitations concerns.

label: Investigation delegated to state authorities with international oversight
original_label: Investigation delegated to state authorities with international oversight
quote: The Ethiopian Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (EAIB) published, on Friday, December 23, 2022, the final report of the investigation into this accident. The Ethiopian authorities had requested the assistance of the BEA for the analysis of the FDR and CVR which were damaged. Following this request, in accordance with the provisions of Annex 13 to the Convention on International Civil Aviation (Annex 13 of the ICAO), the BEA appointed an accredited representative investigator to participate in the investigation conducted by Ethiopia as State of Occurrence.
context: BEA press release explaining the formal investigation structure and responsibility allocation under international aviation protocols.

label: Procedural compliance with international aviation accident investigation rules
original_label: Procedural compliance with international aviation accident investigation rules
quote: ICAO Annex 13 provides that the State conducting the investigation shall send a copy of the draft final report to the participating States (in this case to the accredited representative of the BEA for France and to that of the NTSB for the United States). These States are then invited to provide as soon as possible their significant and substantiated comments on the report.
context: BEA describing the formal procedural requirements governing accident investigation responsibility distribution under international convention.

label: FAA approved Boeing's design and certification
original_label: FAA approved Boeing's design and certification
quote: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is responsible for prescribing minimum standards required in the interest of safety for the design, material, construction, quality of work, and performance of the Airplane, Airplane engines, and propellers (Ref. 49USC44701). Product certification is a regulatory process administered by the FAA to ensure that an Airplane manufacturer's product conforms with Federal Aviation Regulations (FAR). Successful completion of the certification process enables the FAA to issue a Type Certificate (TC) or an Amended Type Certificate.
context: The investigative report documents how Boeing's 737 MAX received FAA Type Certificate approval, placing responsibility for safety clearance on the regulatory authority.

label: Boeing delegated compliance findings to ODA
original_label: Boeing delegated compliance findings to ODA
quote: CP13471 proposed delegation of all Flight Controls Primary & Secondary compliance findings. On April 14, 2015, the FAA approved the delegation of several deliverables; however, they indicated that the deliverable titled '737 Stabilizer System Description and Safety Analysis' (SSA) would be retained by the FAA and will not be proposed for delegation. In November 2016, Boeing submitted the 737 Stabilizer System Description and Safety Analysis (SSA), revision F, to the FAA for acceptance. In December 2016, the FAA's response to Boeing was to 'accept' the submittal and with notation 'delegated SSA approval to ODA.'
context: The report shows how Boeing obtained FAA delegation authority to approve its own safety analyses, shifting responsibility from the regulator to Boeing's ODA.

label: Boeing claimed MCAS hazard classification remained Major despite design changes
original_label: Boeing claimed MCAS hazard classification remained Major despite design changes
quote: In March 2016, Boeing determined that MCAS should be revised to improve wings-level, flaps up, low Mach stall characteristics and identification. The MCAS was revised such that depending on AOA, it would be capable of commanding incremental stabilizer to a maximum of 2.5 degrees at low Mach decreasing to a Maximum of 0.65 degrees at high Mach. Boeing's requirements document indicated that the preliminary functional hazard assessments of MCAS were re-evaluated by pilot assessments in the motion simulator and by engineering analysis and determined to have not changed in hazard classification as a result of the increase in MCAS authority to 2.5 degrees at low speed.
context: Boeing's internal documents show the company concluded that even after significantly increasing MCAS authority (from 0.6 degrees to 2.5 degrees), the hazard classification remained unchanged, minimizing the significance of the design change.

label: Boeing assumptions about pilot recognition of MCAS failures
original_label: Boeing assumptions about pilot recognition of MCAS failures
quote: Unintended stabilizer trim inputs are readily recognized by movement of the stab trim wheel, flight path change or increased column forces. Airplane can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim. Continuous unintended nose down stabilizer trim inputs would be recognized as a Stab Trim or Stab Runaway failure and procedure for Stab Runaway would be followed.
context: Boeing's presentation to the NTSB presenting hazard classification assumed pilots would readily recognize and manage MCAS failures, downplaying the actual difficulty pilots would face.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: MCAS hazard classification based on regulatory compliance assumptions
original_label: MCAS hazard classification based on regulatory compliance assumptions
quote: In a 2019 presentation to the NTSB, Boeing indicated that the MCAS hazard classification of 'major' for uncommanded MCAS function (including up to the new authority limits) in the Normal flight envelope were based on the following conclusions: Unintended stabilizer trim inputs are readily recognized by movement of the stab trim wheel, flight path change or increased column forces. Airplane can be returned to steady level flight using available column (elevator) alone or stabilizer trim.
context: Boeing justified the Major hazard classification for MCAS by citing compliance with regulatory assumptions about pilot capability, treating technical compliance as settling the safety question.

label: FAA retained discretion but approved Boeing's safety analysis
original_label: FAA retained discretion but approved Boeing's safety analysis
quote: Retention and delegation are accomplished with respect to compliance deliverables not to specific functions i.e., MCAS itself would not be delegated to the ODA. Consistent with the FAA authorization, the FAA have discretionary authority as to what is reviewed, whether submitted directly to the FAA for review and approval by an applicant or submitted by a designee or ODA recommending approval. When delegating at the end of a program, there has been some level of FAA involvement and the delegation confirms that the designee should make the final approval.
context: The report documents that while the FAA retained discretionary authority, it approved Boeing's delegated authority to conduct its own safety assessments, placing responsibility back on Boeing.

label: ET302 crew blamed for not understanding MCAS from bulletin
original_label: ET302 crew blamed for not understanding MCAS from bulletin
quote: A thorough study was conducted regarding the airworthiness directive and the FCOM bulletin released after the Lion Air accident. The back ground information from the FCOM bulletin that calls for attention to 'an AOA failure condition that occurs during manual flight only' was assessed during the investigation and was found that it creates confusing to the reader as it appears that the AOA failure condition would only occur during manual flight only. But it was found that the AOA failure condition can occur regardless of the autopilot engagement status and that only activation of MCAS would be dependent on it. There might be a chance that the pilot perceived the bulletin in the above discussed manner and believed the problem would disappear given he engages the autopilot, and the reason for his repetitive attempt to engage the autopilot.
context: The investigation's analysis attributes the captain's actions to possible misunderstanding of the FCOM bulletin wording, framing the crew's response as arising from their interpretation rather than from the bulletin's deficient drafting.

label: Training department relied on Boeing's CBT for MAX differences
original_label: Training department relied on Boeing's CBT for MAX differences
quote: The MAX difference training was CBT training and it's around 6 hours training, maybe 8 hrs there was no simulation training for MAX at all except CBT training. The MAX difference training is CBT training and it is around 2 hours training, maybe if you sit continuously on your laptop for 6 hrs. There was no simulator training at all. The MAX training is 2 hrs CBT training and No Simulator training.
context: Ethiopian Airlines training personnel describe how the airline relied entirely on Boeing's computer-based training for MAX differences, without conducting independent simulator training, delegating responsibility for crew preparation to the manufacturer's training package.

label: Boeing FCTM did not flag MCAS in stall training scenario
original_label: Boeing FCTM did not flag MCAS in stall training scenario
quote: Most approaches to stall training were given in accordance with the Boeing flight crew training manual FCTM guidelines. Per the manual all approaches to stall training were given with the autopilot engaged and the auto throttle disconnected to simulate an approach to stall condition and the pilot initiates recovery by disengaging the autopilot and following the steps in the approach to stall recovery procedure of the QRH. Additionally the investigation also observed that the FCTM doesn't have a guideline on how to conduct an approach to stall training with the autopilot not engaged nor for a stall condition during departure.
context: The investigation found that Boeing's training manual did not address how to handle stall scenarios with autopilot disengaged or during departure, leaving a gap that meant no crew was prepared for the ET302 emergency.

label: MCAS described as stability augmentation rather than trim automation
original_label: MCAS described as stability augmentation rather than trim automation
quote: After the study of various options for addressing this issue, Boeing implemented aerodynamic changes as well as a stability augmentation function called the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), as an extension of the existing Speed Trim System (STS), to improve Airplane handling characteristics and improve static longitudinal stability at elevated angles of attack.
context: Boeing characterized MCAS as a stability augmentation function and extension of the Speed Trim System rather than as an automated nose-down trim system, obscuring its aggressive automated trim behavior.

label: FAA guidance on pilot response used to justify MCAS hazard classification
original_label: FAA guidance on pilot response used to justify MCAS hazard classification
quote: The FHA evaluations were conducted by Boeing in their Engineering Cab using FAA guidance regarding pilot response to flight control failures requiring trim input that is contained in FAA Advisory Circular AC25.7C. In particular, Boeing uses the following assumptions in its flight controls FHAs: Uncommanded system inputs are readily recognizable and can be counteracted by overriding the failure by movement of the flight controls in the normal sense by the flight crew and do not require specific procedures. Action to counter the failure shall not require exceptional piloting skill or strength.
context: Boeing's hazard assessment for MCAS relied on FAA guidance and assumptions about pilot response, allowing Boeing to place the responsibility on pre-existing regulatory standards rather than its own design validation.

label: Boeing believed multiple MCAS inputs could be managed with column alone
original_label: Boeing believed multiple MCAS inputs could be managed with column alone
quote: Boeing indicated that as part of the development process of MCAS, although not formally part of the FHA, engineering personnel and test pilots considered the scenario of multiple MCAS inputs due to pilot trim action following an erroneous AOA input. Their assessment was that each MCAS input could be controlled with column alone and subsequently re-trimmed to zero column force while maintaining the flight path. Five seconds after cessation of the pilot trim command, the subsequent MCAS command could be controlled in the same manner as the previous instance. Eventually, use of the stabilizer cutout switches would be an option to stop the uncommanded stabilizer motion per the runaway stabilizer procedure (which is a trained flight crew memory item).
context: Boeing's internal assessment minimized the challenge of multiple MCAS activations by claiming each could be managed with elevator control alone and that pilots would eventually use the cutout switches, downplaying the actual difficulty and time pressure in the real emergency.

label: Simulator testing of MCAS focused on pilot response, not underlying failure
original_label: Simulator testing of MCAS focused on pilot response, not underlying failure
quote: To perform these simulator tests, Boeing induced a stabilizer trim input that would simulate the stabilizer moving at a rate and duration consistent with the MCAS function. Using this method to induce the hazard resulted in the following motion of the stabilizer trim wheel, increased column forces, and indication that the Airplane was moving nose down. Boeing indicated to the NTSB that this evaluation was focused on the pilot response to uncommanded MCAS operation, regardless of underlying cause. Thus, the specific failure modes that could lead to uncommanded MCAS activation, such as an erroneous high AOA input to the MCAS, were not simulated as part of these functional hazard assessment validation tests. As a result, additional flight deck effects (such as IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE alerts and stick shaker activation) resulting from the same underlying failure (for example, erroneous AOA) were not simulated and were not documented in the stabilizer trim and autoflight safety assessment reports reviewed by the NTSB.
context: The investigation found that Boeing's MCAS testing deliberately simulated only pilot response to trim inputs, not the concurrent flight deck effects that would occur with erroneous AOA, thereby understating the actual emergency complexity.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Ethiopian pilots trained in accordance with Boeing guidelines
original_label: Ethiopian pilots trained in accordance with Boeing guidelines
quote: Records at the airline show both pilots were trained in accordance with Boeing flight crew training guidelines. Thus, in all the training the pilot's received for an approach to stall condition, the crew would start recovery by disengaging the autopilot at the onset of stick shaker and the auto throttle was already disengaged prior to the training maneuver per the FCTM guideline.
context: The investigation notes that Ethiopian Airlines pilots were trained according to Boeing-approved procedures, treating regulatory compliance with the manufacturer's guidelines as satisfactory preparation.

label: Airworthiness Directive compliance delegated to operators
original_label: Airworthiness Directive compliance delegated to operators
quote: ECARAS 5.5.1.2 (d) states that the Authority may issue Airworthiness Directives when it determines that an airframe or aeronautical product has exhibited an unsafe condition and this condition is likely to exist or to develop in other products of the same type design. However, until such time that an appropriate engineering division is established, the Authority will not develop its Airworthiness Directives. With this consideration whenever the State of Design considers that a condition in an Airplane , airframe, Airplane engine, propeller, appliance, or component part is unsafe as shown by the issuance of an airworthiness directive by that State, such directive shall apply to Ethiopian registered civil Airplanes of the type identified in that airworthiness directive. In general, Airworthiness Directives issued by FAA, EASA or both are automatically applicable to all Ethiopian registered Airplanes.
context: Ethiopian aviation regulations establish that the ECAA does not independently certify airworthiness but automatically adopts FAA directives, placing responsibility for aircraft safety on the FAA rather than Ethiopian regulators.

label: Single AOA sensor failure assumed not catastrophic in MCAS FHA
original_label: Single AOA sensor failure assumed not catastrophic in MCAS FHA
quote: For each failure condition, the Airplane architecture (i.e. systems) which implements the function is identified and the high-level system failure conditions are determined. An engineering assessment is performed to verify system failure conditions are being addressed by the individual systems.
context: Boeing's system safety assessment approach examined failure conditions by system architecture, not by the cascading effects of a single erroneous sensor on multiple systems simultaneously, thereby understating the actual hazard.

label: FAA approval delegated design decisions to Boeing
original_label: FAA approval delegated design decisions to Boeing
quote: During discussions and communications with the FAA in 2016, Boeing proposed removing MCAS from the FCOM and the FAA agreed with that recommendation.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing obtained FAA agreement to exclude MCAS from pilot training materials, shifting responsibility for this decision to the regulator.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: MCAS removal justified by regulatory standard
original_label: MCAS removal justified by regulatory standard
quote: FAR 25.1585 provide direction for the content of Airplane operating procedures, such as the AFM. FAR 25.1585(b) states that Information or procedures not directly related to airworthiness or not under the control of the crew must not be included, nor must any procedure that is accepted as basic airmanship. As relevant to this standard, Boeing's rationale for recommending MCAS's removal from the FCOM included that: (1) the MCAS function is automatic and operates in the background, without any control input from the flight crew and (2) Crews were not expected to encounter MCAS in normal operation.
context: Investigation documents Boeing's stated legal reasoning for excluding MCAS from manuals, treating technical compliance with regulations as settling the question.

label: Boeing deferred critical AOA sensor findings to NTSB
original_label: Boeing deferred critical AOA sensor findings to NTSB
quote: According to the report, after the ET302 accident, Boeing informed the NTSB they had made an engineering design error in their initial AOA Sensor Hazard Analysis; Neither Boeing, the NTSB, nor the FAA informed Ethiopian authorities about this critical error that was communicated to the NTSB by Boeing four months earlier.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing informed only the NTSB, not the regulator or affected operators, of a critical design error in AOA sensor analysis.

label: Boeing refused to answer operator safety questions citing ongoing investigation
original_label: Boeing refused to answer operator safety questions citing ongoing investigation
quote: The manufacturer responded on 3 December 2018: declaring I am happy to hear that you were able to take part in the Fleet Team meeting and will attempt to answer other questions from your pilots. However, because of our Annex 13 technical support to the [on-going Lion Air] accident investigation, we are unable to answer questions directly related to this event. I can only address the current system and the Operation's Manual Bulletin. The first two questions directly relate to the accident scenario; therefore, I will be unable to address them here.
context: Boeing's response to Ethiopian Airlines' critical safety questions about MCAS operation and checklist prioritization, declining to provide clarification.

label: Boeing assumed pilots would immediately correct MCAS malfunction
original_label: Boeing assumed pilots would immediately correct MCAS malfunction
quote: In the accident flight crew response assumptions in the initial design process which, coupled with the repetitive MCAS activations, turned out to be incorrect and inconsistent with the FHA classification of Major.
context: Investigation conclusion that Boeing's hazard assessment relied on incorrect assumptions about crew ability to counter MCAS activation.

label: Boeing did not test repetitive MCAS activation in simulation
original_label: Boeing did not test repetitive MCAS activation in simulation
quote: During validation, Boeing considered MCAS activation could occur as a result of erroneous AOA but did not test repetitive erroneous MCAS activations in a flight simulation.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's functional hazard assessment did not validate the actual failure mode that caused both accidents.

label: Boeing assumed elevator control alone would counter MCAS
original_label: Boeing assumed elevator control alone would counter MCAS
quote: Boeing reasoned that such a failure could be countered by using the elevator alone. In addition, stabilizer trim is available to offload column forces, and stabilizer cutout is also available but not required to counter failure. But the associated failures and flight deck effects were not considered in reaching this assessment.
context: Investigation of Boeing's hazard assessment that minimized consequences by assuming manual elevator control would be sufficient.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Boeing blamed design assumptions rather than system design
original_label: Boeing blamed design assumptions rather than system design
quote: While Boeing considered the possibility of uncommanded MCAS activation as part of its FHA, it did not evaluate all the potential alerts and indications that could accompany a failure leading to an uncommanded MCAS.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's assessment compartmentalized failures and did not evaluate integrated flight deck effects.

label: MCAS described as stabilization augmentation function
original_label: MCAS described as stabilization augmentation function
quote: Boeing implemented aerodynamic changes as well as a stability augmentation function called the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), as an extension of the existing Speed Trim System (STS), to improve Airplane handling characteristics and improve static longitudinal stability at elevated angles of attack.
context: Investigation description of how Boeing characterized MCAS, using technical euphemism to describe its nose-down trim function.

label: Pilot training presumed adequate to handle MCAS
original_label: Pilot training presumed adequate to handle MCAS
quote: The investigation found that the Captain's priority remained to control the airplane, which is in line with non-normal situations guideline in the B737 FCTM and the Ethiopian Airlines SOP regarding the prioritization of tasks in case of failure on board. The operator owns training manual which is approved by Ethiopian Civil Aviation Authority. According to this manual the accident pilot and first officer had taken the type rating, recurrent training, line check and proficiency check.
context: Investigation recounting that Boeing and Ethiopian Airlines viewed the accident pilots as having adequate training, shifting focus from system design failures.

label: MCAS authority increased to 2.5 degrees without changing hazard classification
original_label: MCAS authority increased to 2.5 degrees without changing hazard classification
quote: When MCAS authority was increased to 2.5 degrees at low speed, Boeing's requirements document indicated that the preliminary functional hazard assessments of MCAS were re-evaluated by pilot assessments in motion simulator and by engineering analysis and determined to have not changed in hazard classification of Major.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing increased MCAS authority but maintained the same hazard classification, treating the modification as trivial.

label: Boeing did not assess cumulative AOA effects on MCAS
original_label: Boeing did not assess cumulative AOA effects on MCAS
quote: The FCC controlling the MCAS is dependent on a single AOA source and the MCAS contribution to cumulative AOA effects have not been assessed by the manufacturer during the functional hazard assessment.
context: Investigation finding documenting a gap in Boeing's safety analysis regarding integrated system effects.

label: MCAS design assigned single AOA input without redundancy
original_label: MCAS design assigned single AOA input without redundancy
quote: MCAS design on a single AOA inputs made it vulnerable to undesired activation. Its repetitive activation of nose down stabilizer trim made the aircraft uncontrollable.
context: Investigation finding on MCAS design vulnerability, framed as an architectural choice rather than a negligent omission.

label: Multiple flight deck effects termed routine alerts
original_label: Multiple flight deck effects termed routine alerts
quote: The manufacturer did not provide the operator with information and alerts related to MCAS to help them understand the system and know how to resolve potential issues.
context: Investigation statement that Boeing withheld information about MCAS system interaction with other alerts.

label: Hazard assessment minimized pilot workload impact
original_label: Hazard assessment minimized pilot workload impact
quote: The unintended MCAS-commanded stabilizer movement due to erroneous single AOA input was considered a failure condition with Major effect in normal flight envelope. However, this classification did not consider the possibility of the increased workload associated with the additional flight deck effects.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's hazard classification excluded the combined effect of multiple simultaneous alerts on pilot workload.

label: FCOM bulletin placed responsibility on pilots for scenario not disclosed
original_label: FCOM bulletin placed responsibility on pilots for scenario not disclosed
quote: The bulletin instructs the pilot to do the runaway stabilizer NNC for this indication and does not mention any other checklist. FDR data has revealed that the erroneous AOA signal has caused many failures to happen at the same time. When multiple failures occur all together, addressing only one failure scenario would not be enough to handle the situation, but the operational information section of the bulletin tried to direct in handling the situation with only Runaway stabilizer non-normal checklist.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's post-Lion Air bulletin directed pilots to use one procedure for a complex multi-system failure.

label: Production quality defects attributed to intermittent faults rather than design
original_label: Production quality defects attributed to intermittent faults rather than design
quote: A miscalibrated sensor scenario for JT610 and a bird strike scenario for ET302 cannot explain the flight control system alerting, maintenance messages and electrical/electronic system faults that were occurring on these airplanes in the weeks and days before their accidents. These accidents were triggered by production quality defects that presented as intermittent system malfunctions. These types of defects are difficult to identify and troubleshoot. They frequently result in No Fault Found maintenance determinations.
context: Investigation conclusion that AOA sensor failures stemmed from production and electrical issues, not inherent design flaws.

label: Boeing portrayed MCAS as background system outside pilot control
original_label: Boeing portrayed MCAS as background system outside pilot control
quote: As relevant to this standard, Boeing's rationale for recommending MCAS's removal from the FCOM included that: (1) the MCAS function is automatic and operates in the background, without any control input from the flight crew and (2) Crews were not expected to encounter MCAS in normal operation.
context: Boeing's justification for excluding MCAS from pilot manuals, characterizing it as transparent to normal operations.

label: AOA DISAGREE alert implementation treated as optional feature issue
original_label: AOA DISAGREE alert implementation treated as optional feature issue
quote: In 2017, however, within several months after beginning Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries, Boeing identified that the 737 MAX 8 display system software did not correctly implement the AOA DISAGREE alert requirements. As with the Boeing 737 NG, the Boeing display system requirements for the 737 MAX 8 called for the activation of the AOA DISAGREE alert as a standard feature on all Airplanes. The software delivered to Boeing, however, linked the AOA DISAGREE alert to the AOA position indicator, which is an optional feature on the Boeing 737 MAX series. Accordingly, the software activated the AOA DISAGREE alert only if an airline opted for the AOA indicator. At the time of the accident, Boeing advised that the AOA indicator has been selected by approximately 20% of airlines.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's implementation of AOA DISAGREE alert was dependent on optional equipment, minimizing the consequence of single AOA sensor failure.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Boeing deferred MCAS awareness responsibility to pilots
original_label: Boeing deferred MCAS awareness responsibility to pilots
quote: There was CBT training for a few hours long which was supposed to cover the difference between MAX and NG but there was no information related to MCAS description in the system. Instead of focusing on the runaway stabilizer in the AD, the crew would have been aware of MCAS which would have provided them with better understanding of the system and raise their chances of mitigating consequences of repetitive MCAS activations in the accident flight.
context: Investigation recommendation that contrasts Boeing's minimal training with the need for explicit MCAS system awareness.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Interim AD treated as settling safety obligation
original_label: Interim AD treated as settling safety obligation
quote: The AD was presented in 10 parts labeled from (a) to (J). Part (e) unsafe condition: states that the AD was prompted by analysis performed by the manufacturer. Part (h) is AFM revision and it updates the operating procedures in the AFM. Looking at part (h) of the AD, the phrase if relaxing the column causes the trim to move, set stabilizer trim switch to CUTOUT. assumes that there is a possibility for the runaway to be stopped by applying opposite control column force.
context: Investigation analysis showing that the FAA's emergency AD made procedural assumptions not validated by actual accident data.

label: MCAS flap-position dependency omitted from AD and bulletin
original_label: MCAS flap-position dependency omitted from AD and bulletin
quote: MCAS would never have activated repeated nose down trim if the flaps were still left down, even in the presence of erroneous AOA. This critical information was never revealed in the bulletin or in the airworthiness directive.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing withheld crucial system information that would have guided pilot procedures from both regulatory and operator guidance.

label: Erroneous AOA described as triggering uncommanded trim
original_label: Erroneous AOA described as triggering uncommanded trim
quote: In the back ground information of the bulletin, it states that: In the event of erroneous AOA data, the pitch trim system can trim the stabilizer nose down in increments lasting up to 10 seconds. Repetitive cycles of commanded nose down stabilizer continue to occur unless the stabilizer trim system is deactivated through the use of both STAB TRIM CUTOUT switches in accordance with the existing procedure in the runaway stabilizer NNC. As this feature of the pitch trim system is very new information to the FCOM, pilots or the operators, there should have been some description or statement that would explain why the pitch trim system would trim the nose of the airplane down repetitively and what this specific part of the pitch trim system considers as a precondition in order to activate.
context: Investigation critique that Boeing introduced MCAS as merely a feature of the pitch trim system without explaining its hazardous behavior.

label: FAA deferred MCAS safety determinations to Boeing analysis
original_label: FAA deferred MCAS safety determinations to Boeing analysis
quote: Boeing applied for and was granted ODA. Boeing's ODA is authorized to select and appoint individuals to perform some of the delegated functions as representatives of FAA. The delegated functions for a Type Certification (TC) ODA are: establishing and determining conformity of parts, assemblies, installations, test setups, and products (Airplane); finding compliance with airworthiness standards for new design, or major changes to design.
context: Investigation documentation of how the FAA's ODA program allowed Boeing to make compliance determinations for its own design.

label: Boeing did not classify MCAS as safety-critical system
original_label: Boeing did not classify MCAS as safety-critical system
quote: Because uncommanded MCAS function was considered Major, Boeing did not perform a specific fault tree analysis for an uncommanded MCAS hazard and failed to classify MCAS as a safety-critical system, which would have attracted greater FAA analysis during the certification process.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing's hazard classification choice allowed it to avoid rigorous analysis normally required for safety-critical systems.

label: MCAS design validated only under limited conditions
original_label: MCAS design validated only under limited conditions
quote: During the process of developing and validating the Functional Hazard Analysis (FHA), Boeing considered four failure scenarios including uncommanded MCAS function to the Maximum authority limit of 2.5° of stabilizer movement. The uncommanded MCAS function to Maximum authority was flight simulated to high speed Maximum limit of 0.6°, and also the low speed Maximum limit of 2.5° of stabilizer movement and Boeing did not test repetitive erroneous MCAS activations in a flight simulation, but did consider the possibility of an erroneous AOA sensor potentially leading to repeated MCAS activations.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing considered but did not test the actual failure mode that caused both accidents.

label: Boeing informed NTSB but not FAA or operators of AOA sensor design error
original_label: Boeing informed NTSB but not FAA or operators of AOA sensor design error
quote: Boeing has never acknowledged the electrical malfunctions that occurred on both MAX airplanes in the months, weeks, and days leading up to their accidents before MCAS was activated on their fatal flights.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing did not disclose production quality issues affecting AOA sensor electrical systems to operators or regulators.

label: MCAS incremental trim commands presented as safe design feature
original_label: MCAS incremental trim commands presented as safe design feature
quote: MCAS is a function within the Speed Trim System and when activated, moves the stabilizer during flaps up, high angle of attack maneuvers to provide a desirable increase in stick force gradient and improve static longitudinal stability.
context: Boeing's description of MCAS as a desirable stability enhancement, framing its incremental nose-down trim as beneficial.

label: MCAS activation termed reset after pilot electric trim
original_label: MCAS activation termed reset after pilot electric trim
quote: At any time, the stabilizer inputs could be stopped or reversed by the pilots using their yoke-mounted electric stabilizer trim switches, and then the MCAS system will reset after a 5 second delay. The latter behavior is based on the assumption that flight crews use the trim switches to completely return the Airplane to neutral trim.
context: Technical description of MCAS behavior using reset language that obscures the system's latent reactivation after brief pilot input cessation.

label: Stick shaker attributed to normal stall warning function
original_label: Stick shaker attributed to normal stall warning function
quote: If the AOA sensor detects an excessive angle of attack compared to the design characteristic of the 737 MAX 8, the SMYD will activate the stick shaker to provide aural and tactile alert to the flight crew.
context: Technical description of stick shaker function that does not acknowledge its role in masking erroneous AOA sensor signal during MCAS activation.

label: Operators required to implement AD without Boeing system clarification
original_label: Operators required to implement AD without Boeing system clarification
quote: The ECAA issued AD 2018-23-51 dated 08 Nov, 2018 which was released by FAA on November 07, 2018 applicable for 737 MAX-8, 9 Airplanes. The operator was advised to revise its AFM and operating procedures. The ECAA advised the operator implementing the AD and reported to the authority within the specific time provided and this was confirmed by the operator response that has been done accordingly.
context: Investigation account showing that operators were directed to implement procedures for a system they had not been trained on.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Multiple stakeholders shared responsibility for lack of MCAS disclosure
original_label: Multiple stakeholders shared responsibility for lack of MCAS disclosure
quote: The absence of MCAS description in the FCOM, in the flight crew training manual, and the absence of an AOA indicator made it difficultfor the flight crew to identify the problem on the accident Airplane and find the corrective measure to solve.
context: Investigation finding that distributed responsibilities across Boeing, regulators, and operators created gaps in pilot knowledge.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Certification basis applied to derivative aircraft
original_label: Certification basis applied to derivative aircraft
quote: The 737 MAX 8 is a derivative of the 737-800 Model and is part of the 737 MAX families (737 MAX 7, 8, and 941). The 737MAX incorporated the CFM LEAP-1B engine, which has a larger fan diameter and redesigned engine nacelle compared to engines installed on the 737 Next Generation (NG) families. Because the 737-8 is a derivative of the 737-800 model, its certification basis, which was established per 14 CFR 21.101 Changed Product Rule, required Boeing to demonstrate compliance with part 25 as amended by Amendments 25-0 through 25-137, plus amendment 25-141 with exceptions permitted by 14 CFR 21.101for significant areas of change at the product level and those areas affected by the significant product level change.
context: Investigation explaining how Boeing used derivative aircraft certification rules that did not require full reassessment of MCAS as a new system.

label: Boeing relegated MCAS risk mitigation to pilot manual trim capability
original_label: Boeing relegated MCAS risk mitigation to pilot manual trim capability
quote: The investigation assessed documents that Boeing with its knowledge did not mention about MCAS; instead they were telling and emphasizing only the runaway stabilizer/un-commanded stabilizer to the operator and for the authorities. There was CBT training for a few hours long supposed to cover the difference between MAX and NG. There was no information about MCAS description in the system except the Airplane has wide and moved a bit forward body, Size of the Engine which is 84 and the height of the nose gear about 5.6 high.
context: Investigation finding that Boeing directed operators to runaway stabilizer procedures without disclosing MCAS or its recovery requirements.

label: MCAS positioned as standard autopilot function
original_label: MCAS positioned as standard autopilot function
quote: The MCAS function is not incorporated on 737NG Airplanes. If you have further questions, you may contact the appropriate Airline Support Manager.
context: Boeing's Multi-Operator Message treating MCAS as routine autopilot feature rather than novel safety-critical system.

label: Boeing assumed pilot column trim authority sufficient for MCAS recovery
original_label: Boeing assumed pilot column trim authority sufficient for MCAS recovery
quote: The system is designed to allow the flight crew to use column trim switch or stabilizer aisle stand cutout switches to override MCAS input.
context: Boeing's characterization of MCAS design as providing pilot override capability, later contradicted by accident investigation.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Legitimate chronic pain patients need access
original_label: Legitimate chronic pain patients need access
quote: On August 16, 2013, one day after the Board briefing on E2E discussed above, Mortimer D. A. Sackler emailed a Purdue executive and others asking what ideas management had for creating a new distribution system "to help relieve this problem of product access for legitimate chronic pain patients," which would use "an independent service to verify the legitimacy of [the patients'] prescriptions."
context: Sackler family member justifies the development of an alternative distribution strategy as serving a higher purpose of helping legitimate pain patients obtain needed medication.

label: Titration campaign promotes higher dosages
original_label: Titration campaign promotes higher dosages
quote: At the same time, Purdue also refined its marketing message through the S.T.A.R.T. (Supplement, Titrate, Adjust, Reassess, Tailor) initiative by focusing sales conversations with prescribers on titrating patients to dosages. The goal of the program was to discourage patient discontinuation of OxyContin due to perceived lack of pain relief by encouraging providers to increase the OxyContin dosage, or "titrate up."
context: Settlement document describes Purdue's use of euphemistic clinical terminology to frame the strategy of pushing higher opioid doses.

label: Detailing and calling on prescribers
original_label: Detailing and calling on prescribers
quote: Until it stopped marketing opioids in February 2018, Purdue sought to increase and maintain opioid sales by sending sales representatives to prescribers' offices and pharmacies to meet with prescribers in person; deliver company-developed messaging; give the prescribers meals (such as coffee, breakfast, and lunch) and marketing materials (such as articles, brochures, posters, and other media); and provide information about pharmacies stocking Purdue opioids and prescription coverage, including coverage under Federal healthcare benefit programs. This practice is known in the pharmaceutical industry as "calling on" or "detailing" healthcare providers and pharmacies.
context: Settlement document uses sanitized pharmaceutical industry terminology to describe intensive sales targeting of prescribers.

label: Region Zero and Abuse and Diversion Detection program
original_label: Region Zero and Abuse and Diversion Detection program
quote: If Purdue determined a sales representative should not continue to call on a prescriber, the prescriber was placed on the Region Zero list. At all relevant times, Purdue maintained an ADD program, through which Purdue had the means and ability to identify prescribers suspected of engaging in abuse and diversion.
context: Settlement document uses technical acronyms and neutral administrative language to describe Purdue's internal systems for identifying and supposedly excluding problem prescribers.

label: Pseudoaddiction rebranding as dependence
original_label: Pseudoaddiction rebranding as dependence
quote: In addition, representatives were trained to "[o]vercome . . . objection[s]" raised by providers and get physicians to "commit" to prescribe more Purdue products. Specifically, representatives were trained to pivot from legitimate physician concerns about addiction to statements about "dependence" and opioid "tolerance."
context: Settlement describes Purdue sales representatives using euphemistic clinical language to deflect physician concerns about addiction by substituting terms like dependence and tolerance.

label: No ceiling dose framing for high dosages
original_label: No ceiling dose framing for high dosages
quote: When asked about the safety of high dosages, representatives were instructed to respond that OxyContin "does not have a ceiling dose."
context: Sales script uses technical pharmacological language to obscure the safety risks of extremely high opioid dosages.

label: Clinical decision support alerts disguise sales incentive
original_label: Clinical decision support alerts disguise sales incentive
quote: These prompts were known as clinical decision support ("CDS") alerts and were meant to aid the prescriber in making treatment decisions by providing unbiased information consistent with medical practice guidelines. Purdue participated in the design of the Pain CDS alert. It approved the types of patients the Pain CDS would target and what guidance the alert would provide healthcare providers. The Pain CDS was presented to providers as a neutral medical standard.
context: Settlement describes how Purdue disguised its kickback payments to Practice Fusion as clinical decision support when the primary purpose was to increase opioid prescriptions.

label: Reformulated OxyContin still abusable but harder
original_label: Reformulated OxyContin still abusable but harder
quote: In April 2010, Purdue received FDA approval to market a reformulated version of OxyContin. Reformulated OxyContin was more difficult to crush or dissolve, but FDA cautioned that Reformulated OxyContin "is not completely tamper-resistant and those intent on abusing this new formulation will likely find a means to do so. In addition, the product can still be misused or abused and result in overdose by simply administering or ingesting larger than recommended oral doses."
context: Settlement recounts how Purdue could represent the reformulated product as improved without eliminating abuse potential.

label: Board oversight of management strategy
original_label: Board oversight of management strategy
quote: The Sacklers, as members of the Purdue Board, exercised substantial oversight over management's operations of Purdue. For instance, in February of 2011, a memorandum observed: "There seems to be a consensus that the role of the board and that of the management is blurred compared with the distinctions made by other major corporations," and, historically, certain members of Sackler family functioned as "executives, management, board, and shareholders all-in-one [and] worked collaboratively with other managers on a daily basis."
context: Settlement acknowledges Board-level involvement while internal memo suggests responsibility was dispersed through ambiguous roles.

label: FDA approval for medical indication
original_label: FDA approval for medical indication
quote: OxyContin is approved by HHS's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of pain severe enough to require daily, around-the-clock, long-term opioid treatment and for which alternative treatment options are inadequate. It is classified as a Schedule II narcotic under the Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. § 801 et seq.
context: Settlement document cites FDA approval as basis for legitimacy, displacing responsibility to regulatory authority.

label: Sales representatives as intermediaries in detailing decisions
original_label: Sales representatives as intermediaries in detailing decisions
quote: In addition, although Purdue's policy stated that it required timely reporting, Purdue had few, if any, effective compliance measures to address an employee's failure to report, and very few sales representatives were penalized for failing to timely report. Purdue sales representatives were trained to report prescribers suspected of abuse and diversion to ADD, and some sales representatives did so. However, high-volume prescribers were often not reported and, even if they were, they were sometimes not added to Region Zero until they lost the ability to prescribe through legal or medical board action.
context: Settlement describes how Purdue structured incentives and compliance weak enough to displace responsibility for identifying problem prescribers to frontline sales staff.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Consulting company recommendations as independent findings
original_label: Consulting company recommendations as independent findings
quote: On May 28, 2013, Purdue entered into a contract with the consulting company to "conduct a rapid assessment of the underlying drivers of current OxyContin performance, identify key opportunities to increase near-term OxyContin revenue and develop plans to capture priority opportunities." Between July 18 and August 8, 2013, the consulting company provided several reports to a Purdue executive, at least two of which were provided to the Board, including the Sacklers. The consulting company proposed that Purdue adopt what was later referred to as the "Evolve to Excellence" initiative, or "E2E."
context: Settlement describes how Purdue hired external consultants whose recommendations could be cited as independent guidance rather than Purdue's own strategy.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: E2E Executive Oversight Team and Project Management Office
original_label: E2E Executive Oversight Team and Project Management Office
quote: E2E was overseen by the consulting company and some of Purdue's top executives through the creation of the E2E Executive Oversight Team ("EOT") and Project Management Office ("PMO").
context: Settlement notes how responsibility for E2E implementation was dispersed across multiple committees and external consultants.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Sales force incentive structure decouples individuals from outcomes
original_label: Sales force incentive structure decouples individuals from outcomes
quote: In turn, sales representatives were rewarded with incentive compensation tied to the volume of OxyContin prescriptions generated from the health care providers they had detailed and faced corrective action plans, such as performance improvement plans, when they did not meet their sales goals.
context: Settlement describes how incentive compensation systems diffuse individual responsibility by creating structural pressure for outcomes.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: ADD program placed on Region Zero list
original_label: ADD program placed on Region Zero list
quote: Purdue's Abuse and Diversion Detection ("ADD") program and Region Zero list contain examples of high-volume prescribers detailed during E2E that Purdue's own employees suspected were writing medically unnecessary prescriptions. The ADD program began in or around 2002 and ended in or around February 2018. It was governed during most of that time period by Standard Operating Procedure ("SOP") 1.7.1. SOP 1.7.1 instructed Purdue employees to refer prescribers who displayed indicia of abuse and diversion to ADD. Employees referred these prescribers to ADD by issuing a Report of Concern ("ROC").
context: Settlement describes how formal processes and procedures diffused responsibility for identifying problem prescribers across the organization.

label: Abuse limited to insufflation and injection after reformulation
original_label: Abuse limited to insufflation and injection after reformulation
quote: In sum, Purdue knew that, after the release of its Reformulated OxyContin, the product continued to be abused, but the method of abuse shifted to abuse through oral ingestion. Furthermore, Purdue knew that abuse and diversion appeared concentrated among a cohort of high-volume prescribers.
context: Settlement characterizes Purdue's knowledge that abuse shifted from injection to oral ingestion, framing this as a data point rather than a harmful consequence.

label: Decline in high-dose prescriptions among suspected abusers
original_label: Decline in high-dose prescriptions among suspected abusers
quote: Purdue attributed approximately 40% of the decline in OxyContin prescriptions in 2010 to 2011 to "Region Zero" prescribers. Region Zero prescribers were prescribers that Purdue instructed sales representatives not to call on because, based on information maintained by its Abuse and Diversion Detection ("ADD") Program, Purdue determined that "there is a concern about potential abuse or diversion related activities" by them. Purdue had detailed information (down to the number of prescriptions written, product, and dosage) of Purdue products prescribed by all prescribers, including Region Zero doctors from which it could determine that Purdue had been making substantial profits from these prescriptions.
context: Settlement describes how Purdue characterized the loss of high-volume suspicious prescribers as responsible for declining profits, framing illicit use as a business loss metric.

label: Percentage of users reporting OxyContin abuse via oral route
original_label: Percentage of users reporting OxyContin abuse via oral route
quote: The study, which surveyed individuals being treated for opioid use disorder who reported abusing OxyContin through any route, also found that while the overall rate of OxyContin abuse decreased, some users continued to abuse Reformulated OxyContin through insufflation or injection—albeit with more difficulty—and that the percentage of users who reported abusing OxyContin through oral ingestion increased from 54% to 76% following the introduction of Reformulated OxyContin.
context: Settlement recounts study results showing increased oral abuse after reformulation, potentially framing this as acceptable since it was not injection.

label: Patients abusing OxyContin through insufflation and injection
original_label: Patients abusing OxyContin through insufflation and injection
quote: Shortly after the introduction of Reformulated OxyContin, Purdue's profits declined, in large part, because some individuals who abused OxyContin moved to more easily manipulated opioids. Purdue executives closely analyzed Purdue's internal data, including data purchased from vendors, in order to target high-volume prescribers and monitor their prescriptions.
context: Settlement describes Purdue's framing of abusers shifting to other substances as a business problem to be solved through more targeting.

label: Prescribers as problem abusers in Region Zero
original_label: Prescribers as problem abusers in Region Zero
quote: Based on information maintained by its Abuse and Diversion Detection ("ADD") Program, Purdue determined that "there is a concern about potential abuse or diversion related activities" by them. From 2002 through the end of 2012, Purdue conducted various data analyses to identify prescribers with red flags for abuse and diversion. The red flags included prescribers with high numbers of prescriptions for 80mg tablets; prescribers with large numbers of patients that used multiple prescribers or pharmacies; and prescribers with large numbers of cash paying patients.
context: Settlement describes how Purdue categorized high-volume prescribers as the source of abuse and diversion rather than as victims or as vectors of harm.

label: Candyman prescriber blamed for patient abuse
original_label: Candyman prescriber blamed for patient abuse
quote: In June 2010, the sales representative further reported: "the pharmacy manager, says [the doctor] is known as the "Candyman" . . . because she will immediately put every patient on the highest dose of narcotics she can, whether it's Oxycontin or another product. He says when he goes to local pharmacist meetings, when her name comes up everyone in the room cringes and moans because of her practices. He says she is doing all kinds of wacky dosing and tablet strengths. He says he feels like she is not doing what she should be doing with medications. On occasion he has refused to fill prescriptions from her office . . . . He said he's been seeing some crazy dosing of Oxycontin coming in, especially from [Doctor-1]."
context: Call notes depict Doctor-1 using dehumanizing epithets and descriptions rather than professional clinical assessment, deflecting from Purdue's role in detailing her.

label: Doctor-3 clinic indicators of criminal activity
original_label: Doctor-3 clinic indicators of criminal activity
quote: Additionally, Doctor-3's practice had numerous, easily identifiable indicia of abuse and diversion, including large numbers of high dosage patients, long lines of patients waiting outside his clinic, brief or nonexistent patient examinations, and drug transactions in the parking lot. Yet, Doctor-3 was not placed on Region Zero during this time period and sales representatives were directed to continue calling on him.
context: Settlement describes obvious indicators of criminal activity at Doctor-3's clinic, framing them as characteristics of a bad actor rather than as evidence of Purdue's complicity in continued detailing.

label: Patient death attributed to reformulated product rejection
original_label: Patient death attributed to reformulated product rejection
quote: Purdue sales representatives' call notes also identified ongoing concerns regarding abuse by the doctor's patients. For example, a 2010 call note stated: "Had a patient that died this week that was taking OxyContin (2 tablets of 80mg at Q12h). She was 45-48 years old and had been seen by [the doctor] for 10 years. The patient had complained previously (was reported) that the reformulation made her sick and tried to get a refund for the reformulation (the pharmacy refused). She did find generic OxyContin. Patient was found dead sitting at the kitchen table with a syringe beside her. It has been ruled as an accidental death by the police."
context: Call note records a patient death with no indication of accountability, framing it as an isolated incident rather than evidence of harm from high-dose prescribing.

label: Increased DEA and pharmacy scrutiny as sales obstacle
original_label: Increased DEA and pharmacy scrutiny as sales obstacle
quote: For example, a Business Condition Report from a May 2-3, 2013 Board of Directors Meeting described sales as being "$144mm behind Q12013 budget" with "$36mm attributed to lower Rx demand" and stated that "[p]ossible causes of fewer tabs/Rx in the market" include "Increased State Regulations"; "Anti-opioid environment"; and "Increased DEA/law enforcement scrutiny of physicians, pharmacies and wholesalers."
context: Board presentation frames law enforcement efforts and state regulations as business obstacles rather than legitimate safeguards, implicitly questioning their legitimacy.

label: Pharmacist scrutiny as retail channel risk
original_label: Pharmacist scrutiny as retail channel risk
quote: In 2013, the consulting company informed Purdue and its Board, that "[t]he retail channel, both pharmacies and distributors, is under intense scrutiny and direct risk." More specifically, the consulting company explained "[t]here are reports of wholesalers stopping shipments entirely to an increasing number of pharmacies," "[m]any wholesalers are also imposing hard quantity limits on orders based on prior purchase levels," and "[p]harmacy chains are implementing guidelines for which patients can fill opioid prescriptions."
context: Consulting report frames pharmacist safeguards against medically unnecessary prescriptions as threats to Purdue's business model.

label: Pharmacist daily decisions as access issue
original_label: Pharmacist daily decisions as access issue
quote: In 2013, the same consulting company that developed E2E identified pharmacist scrutiny as a hurdle to sales and told the Board: "Access to OxyContin for some patients has become quite challenging in specific local markets. This is due to a combination of factors including: regulations, DEA initiatives, [Physicians for Responsible Opioid Prescribing], wholesaler initiatives and local pharmacist perceptions. . . While the wholesaler issues are quite visible and real, we believe the daily decisions being made at local pharmacies, while less publicly visible, are in fact creating far greater access issues."
context: Consulting company frames pharmacist professional judgment as creating unjustified access barriers rather than as appropriate control of medically unnecessary prescriptions.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Alternative distribution for patient access
original_label: Alternative distribution for patient access
quote: Shortly thereafter, the Sacklers approved E2E, and the E2E program went on to develop "multiple tactics to address these issues," including "alternative supply channels." In 2015, the Company entered agreements with three specialty pharmacies. Some of the prescriptions that were filled by the specialty pharmacies had been rejected by traditional retail pharmacies and displayed indicia that the prescriptions were not for a medically accepted indication; for uses that were unsafe, ineffective, and medically unnecessary; and that were often diverted for uses that lacked a legitimate medical purpose.
context: Settlement describes how Purdue justified alternative distribution as addressing access, even when filling prescriptions that traditional pharmacies had rejected as inappropriate.

label: Evolve to Excellence initiative rebranding sales targeting
original_label: Evolve to Excellence initiative rebranding sales targeting
quote: The consulting company proposed that Purdue adopt what was later referred to as the "Evolve to Excellence" initiative, or "E2E."
