category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Defeat device exceptions provide legal cover
original_label: Defeat device exceptions provide legal cover
quote: some manufacturers decrease the effectiveness of ECTs outside specific thermal windows close to the temperature range prescribed by the NEDC test, claiming that such a decrease is necessary to protect the engine against damage in line with the derogations to the ban on defeat devices provided for in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007
context: Manufacturers cited existing legal exceptions to the defeat device ban to justify thermal modulation strategies, treating statutory derogations as technical compliance.

label: Measurement uncertainty justifies excess emissions
original_label: Measurement uncertainty justifies excess emissions
quote: It is debatable, as confirmed by several experts, whether there is a need to include any conformity factor in the RDE procedure, given that they remain in clear contradiction with the results of several independent tests carried out on Euro 6 cars, which showed that NOx conformity factors below the value of 1.5 or even much lower than 1 are already achievable.
context: The report notes that conformity factors permitting 50-110% excess emissions were justified by citing measurement uncertainty, despite evidence such tolerance was unnecessary.

label: Optimization strategies for test passage
original_label: Optimization strategies for test passage
quote: optimisation strategies put in place by car manufacturers to pass the laboratory test by calibrating vehicles ECTs so that their effectiveness is only ensured within the boundary conditions of the NEDC test
context: The report uses the term 'optimization strategies' which manufacturers employed, a technical framing that obscures deliberate calibration to perform well only during testing.

label: Auxiliary emission strategies
original_label: Auxiliary emission strategies
quote: the requirement to disclose the auxiliary emission strategies, which change the base strategies for a specific purpose and in response to a specific set of ambient or operating conditions, was not provided for in the legislation until April 2016
context: The term 'auxiliary emission strategies' euphemistically describes software that activates test-detection and deactivates emissions controls under real-world conditions.

label: Cycle beating and hard cycle beating
original_label: Cycle beating and hard cycle beating
quote: The official in DG GROW who replied to the e-mail, with DG ENV and DG MOVE in copy, stated that this is very useful and a clear case of hard cycle beating
context: Internal Commission correspondence used the technical term 'hard cycle beating' to describe what was evidence of prohibited defeat device operation.

label: Real-world emissions not proportional to public health harm
original_label: Real-world emissions not proportional to public health harm
quote: There are large discrepancies between the NOx emissions of most Euro 3-6 diesel cars measured during the type-approval process with the New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) laboratory test, which meet the legal emission limit, and their NOx emissions measured in real driving conditions, which substantially exceed the limit. Those discrepancies affect the vast majority of diesel cars and are not limited to the Volkswagen vehicles equipped with prohibited defeat devices. These discrepancies contribute, to a large extent, to infringements by several Member States of Directive 2008/50/EC
context: Testimony and evidence indicate that massive, widespread real-world emissions violations caused widespread air quality violations, but these were often treated as technical compliance issues rather than public health failures.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: No law forbids thermal windows before scandal
original_label: No law forbids thermal windows before scandal
quote: The scope and provisions of the ban on defeat devices has never been disputed by anyone. No Member State or car manufacturer ever questioned or asked for clarification on the provisions on defeat devices, including the implementation of the ban, until the Volkswagen case.
context: Manufacturers and regulators justified pre-scandal inaction by claiming the law was clear and undisputed, treating absence of clarification as evidence the conduct was lawful.

label: Member States failed to enforce law
original_label: Member States failed to enforce law
quote: Member States contravened their legal obligation to monitor and enforce the ban on defeat devices set out in Article 5(2) of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007. None of them found the defeat devices installed in the Volkswagen vehicles, in particular those Member States whose authorities type-approved those vehicles.
context: The inquiry places enforcement responsibility on Member States, whose failure to act is characterized as the primary legal violation rather than manufacturer misconduct.

label: Type-approval authority bears conformity checking duty
original_label: Type-approval authority bears conformity checking duty
quote: The Member States should have ensured that their type-approval authorities have sufficient human and financial resources to perform in-house testing. They should have not relied on tests performed in the car manufacturers' certified laboratories under the supervision of technical services.
context: The report attributes responsibility for detecting false emissions data to Member State authorities rather than placing duties on manufacturers to disclose or certify accuracy.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: JRC findings not conveyed to leadership
original_label: JRC findings not conveyed to leadership
quote: The Commission should have ensured that the JRC's research findings and concerns discussed among the Commission services with regard to possible illegal practices by manufacturers reached the higher levels of the hierarchy which allegedly did not happen so that appropriate action could be taken.
context: The Commission's inaction is defended on grounds that damaging information about manufacturers allegedly never reached top decision-makers, diffusing responsibility across organizational layers.

label: Defeat devices affect only fraction of fleet
original_label: Defeat devices affect only fraction of fleet
quote: defeat devices were generally not considered among the possible reasons behind the discrepancies between laboratory and on-road NOx emissions
context: Before 2015, deliberate defeat devices were treated as irrelevant to understanding emissions violations, minimizing their culpability by suggesting they explained only a small part of the problem.

label: Technical complexity prevents defeat device detection
original_label: Technical complexity prevents defeat device detection
quote: Experts have noted the consensus view that the pre-emptive checking and possible detection of a fraudulent emissions system defeat device through unrestricted access to the vehicle's proprietary software is not a viable method, due to the extreme complexity of such software.
context: Technical experts justified the absence of pre-scandal defeat device detection by claiming software analysis was impractical, placing responsibility on technical limitations rather than institutional failure.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Lack of explicit criteria for defeat device exceptions
original_label: Lack of explicit criteria for defeat device exceptions
quote: Some experts and witnesses and some Member States questioned the level of clarity of the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) of the Euro 5/6 regulation and pointed out the lack of a list of assessment criteria to evaluate whether emission control strategies used by car manufacturers are instances of prohibited defeat devices or can be justified on grounds of engine protection and safety
context: Manufacturers and regulators defended thermal modulation and other strategies by citing the absence of explicit regulatory criteria defining prohibited conduct, treating ambiguity as legal permission.

label: Voluntary recalls rectify defective vehicles
original_label: Voluntary recalls rectify defective vehicles
quote: German Federal Minister Alexander Dobrindt stated that Volkswagen agreed to a voluntary recall with the national type-approval authority because of the imminent withdrawal of type-approval for vehicles illegally using a defeat device. Volkswagen representatives stated that the recall would bring the affected vehicles into line with the type-approval certification while keeping the essential durability, quality and efficiency parameters unchanged.
context: Volkswagen minimized the harm of defeat devices by claiming recalls would restore compliance without performance loss, treating a serious violation as fully remediable.

label: PEMS measurement uncertainty comparable to industry uncertainty
original_label: PEMS measurement uncertainty comparable to industry uncertainty
quote: The maximum additional measurement uncertainty of PEMS for light-duty vehicles with respect to laboratory tests has been steadily decreasing and is currently at about 30 %, and the average uncertainty was estimated by the Commission to be 18.75 %, with a concrete possibility of reaching 10-15 % within a short period of time
context: The justification for high conformity factors (1.5-2.1 permitting 50-110% excess emissions) rests on comparing them to PEMS measurement uncertainty of 18.75%, implying the allowances were technically reasonable.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Prioritizing particulate matter reduction in Euro 5
original_label: Prioritizing particulate matter reduction in Euro 5
quote: However, the Artemis test cycle was not designed for type-approval testing, but rather for emissions inventory, and therefore it would have required adaptations in order to be used in type-approval procedures. Nevertheless, the main priority was to achieve a timely reduction of the emissions of carcinogenic PM
context: Legislators justified not updating the emissions test procedure by citing the urgent need to reduce particulate matter via Euro 5 standards, treating delay in realistic NOx testing as serving a higher environmental priority.

label: Memory effect in engine strategy
original_label: Memory effect in engine strategy
quote: The e-mail also mentions a memory effect that was found to influence the engine strategy for at least 20 minutes after starting the engine at a specific temperature.
context: Internal Commission correspondence used the technical term 'memory effect' to describe software behavior that activated emissions controls during the test period and then deactivated them after.

label: Retrofitting affects durability and efficiency
original_label: Retrofitting affects durability and efficiency
quote: Some experts questioned whether the proposed recall measures would not impact the durability and efficiency of the affected vehicles.
context: Testimony suggested that fixing defeat devices would harm vehicle performance, implicitly arguing that the violations should be tolerated to preserve consumer benefits.

label: Industry pressure and consensus delayed RDE
original_label: Industry pressure and consensus delayed RDE
quote: witnesses argued that, rather than political interference, delays were due to the fact that decision-making at EU level is a consensus-building process that takes time, that administrative processes are often unable to keep up with technological development, and that the focus of the EU and the Member States was on avoiding burdens on the industry after the crisis started in 2008
context: Witnesses justified years of delay in developing realistic emissions testing by blaming structural features of EU governance, technological development timelines, and post-crisis policy priorities rather than industry obstruction.

label: Not-to-exceed concept as normal regulation
original_label: Not-to-exceed concept as normal regulation
quote: the development of a new, more realistic, laboratory test procedure, the so-called 'Worldwide harmonised Light vehicles Test Procedure' (WLTP), due to replace the obsolete NEDC, has taken an extremely long time. The test will be mandatory as part of the type-approval process of all new vehicle types as of 1 September 2017 and for all new vehicles one year later.
context: The report treats the years-long delay in introducing realistic testing as normal regulatory process rather than institutional failure to respond to known, serious violations.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Commission proposal for conformity factors within legal power
original_label: Commission proposal for conformity factors within legal power
quote: In its initial draft for the second RDE package, the Commission had proposed to the TCMV conformity factors towards the lower end of the 1.6-2.2 range for the first phase and of the 1.2-1.6 range for the second phase
context: The Commission's proposal to permit vehicles to exceed legal NOx limits by 60-120% was framed as a technical regulatory measure within its delegated authority, treating the excess as formally lawful.

label: Emissions discrepancies known but not acted upon
original_label: Emissions discrepancies known but not acted upon
quote: The existence of the discrepancies, and their significant negative impact on attaining air quality objectives, in particular with regard to urban areas, had been known to the Commission, to the responsible authorities of the Member States and to many other stakeholders since at least 2004-2005 when Regulation (EC) No 715/2007 was being prepared.
context: The report documents that massive, city-level air quality violations were common knowledge for over a decade, yet treated as inevitable rather than as grounds for enforcement action.

label: Emissions within normal driving parameters not enforced
original_label: Emissions within normal driving parameters not enforced
quote: Member States did not monitor and enforce appropriately the application of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007, notably in contravention of Article 5(1) on the obligation for manufacturers to design, construct and assemble cars so as to enable them to comply with the regulation in normal use when driving on European roads and not only in laboratory conditions. Yet, a former rapporteur on emissions and type-approval legislation made very clear that Parliament never intended to restrict normal use to the narrow conditions under which cars are tested in the laboratory for type approval. He indicated that driving conditions as commonly encountered when driving on European roads (including differences in temperature, altitude, engine load, vehicle speed, etc.) were meant to be considered as normal use.
context: The report notes that regulators failed to enforce the statutory obligation that vehicles comply in normal driving, implicitly blaming drivers' varied driving conditions rather than manufacturers' design choices for emissions violations.

label: Defeat device disguised as acoustic function
original_label: Defeat device disguised as acoustic function
quote: VW employees acting at the direction of DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators designed, created, and implemented a software function (the "defeat device") to cheat the standard U.S. emissions tests. DORENKAMP, HADLER, and their co-conspirators referred to the software as, among other things, the "acoustic function," "switch logic," "cycle beating," or "emissions-tight mode."
context: The indictment describes how VW engineers used sanitized technical terminology to disguise the defeat device software.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Strategic goal of selling diesel in US market
original_label: Strategic goal of selling diesel in US market
quote: Selling diesel vehicles in the U.S. market was an important strategic goal of VW AG. This project became known within VW as the "US'07'' project.
context: The indictment notes that VW presented diesel vehicle sales as a strategic corporate objective, potentially framing the wrongdoing as necessary to achieve this goal.

label: Engineers authorized to use defeat device by DORENKAMP
original_label: Engineers authorized to use defeat device by DORENKAMP
quote: Throughout in or around 2006, DORENKAMP authorized VW engineers to use the defeat device in the development of the US'07 project, despite concerns expressed by certain VW AG employees about the propriety of designing and activating the defeat device software.
context: The indictment describes how DORENKAMP's authorization placed responsibility for the defeat device decision with a senior leader rather than the engineers implementing it.

label: HADLER authorized continuation despite knowing of defeat device
original_label: HADLER authorized continuation despite knowing of defeat device
quote: As a result of the meeting, HADLER authorized DORENKAMP to proceed with the US'07 project despite knowing that only the use of the defeat device software would enable VW diesel vehicles to pass U.S. emissions tests.
context: The indictment indicates HADLER's explicit authorization of the defeat device, shifting responsibility upward in the chain of command.

label: Steering wheel angle recognition as detection feature
original_label: Steering wheel angle recognition as detection feature
quote: By making these alterations to the operation of the defeat device, the conspirators ensured that the 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles would almost never be driven on the road in an emissions-compliant manner.
context: Technical language ('steering wheel angle recognition') disguises the true function of improving the defeat device's ability to detect when a vehicle is undergoing a test.

label: Software update framed as improvement
original_label: Software update framed as improvement
quote: NEUSSER and other co-conspirators falsely and fraudulently represented, and/or caused others to represent, to U.S. regulators, U.S. customers and others that the software update in or around 2014 was intended to improve the 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles when, in fact, the defendants and other co-conspirators knew that the update used the steering wheel angle of the vehicle as a basis to better detect when the vehicle was undergoing emissions tests, thereby improving the defeat device's precision in order to reduce the stress on the exhaust system.
context: The indictment describes how a software update designed to perfect the defeat device was publicly marketed as a straightforward improvement to vehicle performance.

label: NEUSSER authorized steering wheel angle function
original_label: NEUSSER authorized steering wheel angle function
quote: In or about April 2013, NEUSSER authorized activation of the software underlying the steering wheel angle recognition function. VW employees then installed the new software function in new 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles being sold in the United States, and later installed it in existing 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles through software updates during routine vehicle maintenance.
context: NEUSSER's authorization placed decision-making responsibility with a senior executive rather than with technical staff.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Task force formed to formulate responses
original_label: Task force formed to formulate responses
quote: In response to learning the results of the ICCT study, engineers in the VW Brand Engine Development department formed an ad hoc task force to formulate responses to questions that arose from the U.S. regulators. VW AG employees, including NEUSSER, GOTTWEIS, SCHMIDT, PETER, and their co-conspirators, determined not to disclose to U.S. regulators that the tested vehicle models operated with a defeat device.
context: The indictment describes how responsibility for concealment was distributed across a task force and multiple senior employees rather than assigned to individuals.

label: False fixes and explanations without revealing defeat device
original_label: False fixes and explanations without revealing defeat device
quote: Throughout 2014 and the first half of 2015, NEUSSER, GOTTWEIS, SCHMIDT, PETER, and their co-conspirators, continued to offer, and cause to be offered, software and hardware "fixes" and explanations to U.S. regulators for the 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles' higher NOx measurements on the road without revealing the underlying reason - the existence of software designed to detect, evade and defeat U.S. emissions tests.
context: VW leaders used sanitized language of technical 'fixes' and 'explanations' to obscure the core deception about the defeat device.

label: Irregularities and abnormalities without naming cheating
original_label: Irregularities and abnormalities without naming cheating
quote: SCHMIDT attempted to and did mislead and deceive CARB by offering technical reasons and excuses such as "irregularities" or "abnormalities" for the discrepancy without revealing the fundamental reason for the higher NOx measurements on the road: software intentionally installed in VW vehicles to detect, evade, and defeat U.S. emissions testing.
context: SCHMIDT used vague technical terminology to obscure the deliberate cheating mechanism to regulators.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Instructions to destroy incriminating document
original_label: Instructions to destroy incriminating document
quote: In or around July 2012, engineers from the VW Brand Engine Development department met, in separate meetings, with GOTTWEIS and NEUSSER to explain that they suspected the cause of the hardware failures in the Subject Vehicles was the increased stress on the exhaust system from being driven too long in "dyno" mode as a result of the use of software designed to detect, evade, and defeat U.S. emission tests. To illustrate the software's function, the engineers used a document. Although GOTTWEIS and NEUSSER understood the purpose and significance of the software, they each encouraged further concealment of the software. Specifically, GOTTWEIS and NEUSSER each instructed the engineers who presented the issue to them to destroy the document used to illustrate the operation of the cheating software.
context: Senior leaders shifted responsibility to lower-level engineers to destroy evidence while the leaders themselves remained insulated from the act.

label: HADLER instructed never to present or distribute defeat device slides
original_label: HADLER instructed never to present or distribute defeat device slides
quote: On or about October 17, 2007, another version of a backup slide containing software changes that made numerous references to explicit engineering terms for the defeat device was exchanged with HADLER, DORENKAMP, and others. In response, on or about the same date, HADLER wrote (in German) that "we shall please never present this anywhere and will also not distribute it."
english_gloss: "we shall please never present this anywhere and will also not distribute it."
context: HADLER, as a senior leader, directed that evidence of the defeat device be concealed, placing responsibility for information control with him.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Promoting vehicles as green diesel
original_label: Promoting vehicles as green diesel
quote: On or about November 18, 2007, HADLER sent an email to DORENKAMP and others attaching three photos of himself with California's then-Governor, which were taken during an event at which HADLER promoted the 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles in the United States as "green diesel."
context: HADLER promoted the diesel vehicles as environmentally beneficial, potentially framing the project as serving a higher environmental purpose.

label: Clean diesel marketing campaign
original_label: Clean diesel marketing campaign
quote: Starting on or about July 1, 2008, defendants marketed and sold in the U.S. the Subject Vehicles containing the new "clean diesel" engine, which, in fact, contained the defeat device. A marketing vehicle was painted with green vines and the words "Jetta TDI Clean Diesel" and "goodcleandieselfun.com."
context: VW used marketing language and imagery designed to obscure the true nature of vehicles equipped with hidden defeat devices.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: SCHMIDT restricts knowledge to contain leak
original_label: SCHMIDT restricts knowledge to contain leak
quote: On or about April 15, 2014, SCHMIDT forwarded GOTTWEIS a copy of the ICCT presentation, and an email chain in which a VW employee stated, "[s]ome presenters indicated that they suspected cheating, where the vehicle recognizes it is an [sic] a dyno and runs different calibration that [sic] what it runs in actual driving. We will have to be careful with this going forward." In his cover email, SCHMIDT concluded with, "Within VW GOA, the study is known only to EEO, and we want to keep it that way for the time being."
context: SCHMIDT attempted to limit the spread of knowledge about the defeat device among VW employees, diffusing responsibility by restricting information flow.

label: Full explanation impossible; new software cannot make cars compliant
original_label: Full explanation impossible; new software cannot make cars compliant
quote: On or about May 22, 2014, GOTTWEIS sent a VW AG executive a memorandum describing a timeline of events with CARB after the ICCT study. GOTTWEIS stated that a full explanation could not be provided to authorities and it could be assumed that the authorities would test the vehicles for defeat devices. GOTTWEIS stated that even new software would not be able to make the cars fully compliant.
context: GOTTWEIS acknowledged in internal communications that the problem could not be solved through legitimate technical fixes, implicitly acknowledging the severity and intractability of the wrongdoing.

label: False reasons for discrepancies in NOx emissions
original_label: False reasons for discrepancies in NOx emissions
quote: On or about October 1, 2014, VW employees presented to CARB regarding the ICCT study results and discrepancies identified in NOx emissions between dynamometer testing and road driving. In responding to questions, VW employees did not reveal that the existence of the defeat device was the explanation for the discrepancies in NOx emissions, and, in fact, gave CARB false reasons for the discrepancies in NOx emissions including driving patterns and technical issues.
context: VW employees used vague, alternative explanations ('driving patterns,' 'technical issues') to disguise the deliberate defeat device.

label: Proposing misleading arguments to counter emissions tests
original_label: Proposing misleading arguments to counter emissions tests
quote: On or about May 12, 2015, PETER sent an email to VW AG employees referencing on-road emissions measurements by CARB in mid-April through June. PETER proposed possible misleading and false arguments to present to CARB as to why the vehicles were not passing the emissions tests on the road.
context: PETER used euphemistic framing ('arguments,' 'reasons') for what were deliberate deceptive statements to regulators.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Need for good arguments to counter regulator questions
original_label: Need for good arguments to counter regulator questions
quote: On or about June 23, 2015, PETER sent an email to VW AG employees reiterating that VW AG needed to come up with "good arguments" to counter the questions from the U.S. regulators.
context: PETER framed the concealment strategy as a collective enterprise requiring group problem-solving, diffusing individual responsibility.

label: Employee excluded to avoid conscious lying
original_label: Employee excluded to avoid conscious lying
quote: On or about August 17, 2015, SCHMIDT wrote to a manager at VW that another manager had just "explained to me on the telephone why [another VW employee] should not come along [to a future CARB meeting] - so he would not have to consciously lie."
context: Management took responsibility for deciding who would participate in deceptive communications, protecting lower-level employees from direct involvement.

label: Script for continued concealment approved by management
original_label: Script for continued concealment approved by management
quote: On or about August 18, 2015, NEUSSER and his co-conspirators approved a script to be followed by VW employees during an upcoming meeting with CARB on or about August 19, 2015. The script provided for continued concealment of the defeat device from CARB in the 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles, with the goal of obtaining approval to sell the model year 2016 2.0 Liter Subject Vehicles in the United States.
context: Management framed deliberate deception as a prepared 'script,' using bureaucratic language to distance themselves from the falsifications.

label: Signed statement that emissions systems will not cause unreasonable risk
original_label: Signed statement that emissions systems will not cause unreasonable risk
quote: The Volkswagen Group states that any element of design, system, or emission control device installed on or incorporated in the Volkswagen Group's new motor vehicles or new motor vehicle engines for the purpose of complying with standards prescribed under section 202 of the Clean Air Act, will not, to the best of the Volkswagen Group's information and belief, cause the emission into the ambient air of pollutants in the operation of its motor vehicles or motor vehicle engines which cause or contribute to an unreasonable risk to public health or welfare except as specifically permitted by the standards prescribed under section 202 of the Clean Air Act.
context: The indictment quotes VW's formal certification statement to the EPA, using technical, legalistic language that masks the intentional inclusion of defeat devices.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Pain relief and patient access messaging
original_label: Pain relief and patient access messaging
quote: Initiatives from the groups in this report often echoed and amplified messages favorable to increased opioid use—and ultimately, the financial interests of opioid manufacturers. These groups have issued guidelines and policies minimizing the risk of opioid addiction and promoting opioids for chronic pain, lobbied to change laws directed at curbing opioid use, and argued against accountability for physicians and industry executives responsible for overprescription and misbranding.
context: Senate report characterizing how advocacy groups justified opioid promotion by framing it as advancing patient access to pain relief.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Patient access and pain management as rationale
original_label: Patient access and pain management as rationale
quote: According to a complaint from the City of Chicago, for example, the American Academy of Pain Medicine and the American Pain Society issued a consensus statement in 1997 which endorsed opioids to treat chronic pain and claimed that the risk that patients would become addicted to opioids was low.
context: Report documenting how medical professional societies justified opioid endorsement on patient care grounds.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Protecting vulnerable patient populations
original_label: Protecting vulnerable patient populations
quote: Similarly, the American Geriatrics Society released guidelines in 2009 for the management of persistent pain in older patients. While acetaminophen remained the preferred option for the treatment of chronic pain patients, the American Geriatrics Society recommended opioids—as opposed to aspirin or ibuprofen—for those unable to gain relief from Tylenol and similar products. According to the City of Chicago complaint, the guidelines included these recommendations: All patients with moderate to severe pain . . . should be considered for opioid therapy (low quality of evidence, strong recommendation), and the risks [of addiction] are exceedingly low in older patients with no current or past history of substance abuse.
context: Report citing advocacy group guidance that framed opioid therapy as serving vulnerable elderly patients.

label: Pseudoaddiction concept minimizing addiction risk
original_label: Pseudoaddiction concept minimizing addiction risk
quote: The American Academy of Pain Medicine and the American Pain Society also allegedly issued guidelines in 2009 that promote[d] opioids as safe and effective for treating chronic pain, despite acknowledging limited evidence, and conclude[d] that the risk of addiction is manageable for patients regardless of past abuse histories.
context: Report documenting how professional societies used sanitized language to characterize addiction risk as manageable.

label: Addiction risk claimed to be low or rare
original_label: Addiction risk claimed to be low or rare
quote: According to the City of Chicago complaint, the guidelines included these recommendations: All patients with moderate to severe pain . . . should be considered for opioid therapy (low quality of evidence, strong recommendation), and the risks [of addiction] are exceedingly low in older patients with no current or past history of substance abuse. The American Geriatrics Society also partnered with the American Academy of Pain Medicine and Janssen to create the 2009 patient education guide entitled, Finding Relief: Pain Management for Older Adults, which stated that [m]any studies show that opioids are rarely addictive when used properly for the management of chronic pain.
context: Report quoting advocacy group and patient education materials that minimized addiction risks.

label: Addiction risk characterized as exceedingly low
original_label: Addiction risk characterized as exceedingly low
quote: According to a complaint from the City of Chicago, for example, the American Academy of Pain Medicine and the American Pain Society issued a consensus statement in 1997 which endorsed opioids to treat chronic pain and claimed that the risk that patients would become addicted to opioids was low.
context: Report documenting medical professional societies' minimization of addiction consequences.

label: Manufacturers' responsibilities shifted to doctor judgment
original_label: Manufacturers' responsibilities shifted to doctor judgment
quote: In defense of Dr. Hurwitz, the National Pain Foundation suggested that [t]he conviction [in the trial court] broke ground by holding that a doctor acting in the good faith belief that he was serving the best medical interest of his patient could be found to be a drug dealer.
context: Report quoting advocacy group amicus brief displacing responsibility from physician overprescriber to legal system.

label: CDC guidelines attacked as procedurally illegitimate
original_label: CDC guidelines attacked as procedurally illegitimate
quote: Similarly, several advocacy groups criticized draft guidelines in 2015, arguing that the CDC slides presented on Wednesday were not transparent relative to process and failed to disclose the names, affiliations, and conflicts of interest of the individuals who participated in the construction of these guidelines. Dr. Richard Payne, a physician affiliated with the Center for Practical Bioethics, made a similar argument, criticizing the CDC guidelines as the product of conflicts of interests in terms of biases [and] intellectual conflicts.
context: Report documenting how advocacy groups attacked the credibility of CDC guideline development process.

label: CDC accused of secrecy and bias
original_label: CDC accused of secrecy and bias
quote: The Washington Legal Foundation also strongly criticized the guidelines on procedural grounds, claiming CDC had developed its guidelines in an overly secretive manner and in violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, which called into question the viability of the entire enterprise. The Washington Legal Foundation claimed, moreover, that [s]tate governments and the medical community are unlikely to accept any guidelines tainted by charges that they were prepared in secret without meaningful stakeholder input.

original_label: Accounting hedges versus economic hedges distinction obscured

original_label: Structuring fees and guaranty fees mask capital transfers

The approval process reflected a model in which Enron's business units were in full command of transactions and had the time and motivation to find the highest price for assets they were selling. In some cases, transactions were consistent with this model, but in many of the transactions the assumptions underlying this model did not apply.
context: Powers Report describes how formal approval procedures and documentation processes were treated as legitimating even economically questionable transactions.

label: Investors blamed for not reading footnotes
original_label: Investors blamed for not reading footnotes
quote: The disclosures also asserted that the related-party transactions were reasonable compared to transactions with third parties, apparently without any factual basis. The process by which the relevant disclosures were crafted was influenced substantially by Enron Global Finance (Fastow's group). There was an absence of forceful and effective oversight by Senior Enron Management and in-house counsel, and objective and critical professional advice by outside counsel at Vinson & Elkins, or auditors at Andersen. Investors who 'should have read the footnotes'
context: Powers Report notes the implicit blame of investors for not detecting the misleading disclosures in the footnotes.

label: Questioning of short-seller motives or bias
original_label: Questioning of short-seller motives or bias
quote: The fundamental flaw in these transactions was not that the price was too low. Instead, as a matter of economic substance, it is not clear that anything was really being bought or sold. Controls that were directed at assuring a fair price to Enron were ineffective to address this problem.

label: Vinson & Elkins investigation predetermined by scope
original_label: Vinson & Elkins investigation predetermined by scope
quote: The result of the V&E review was largely predetermined by the scope and nature of the investigation and the process employed. We identified the most serious problems in the Raptor transactions only after a detailed examination of the relevant transactions and, most importantly, discussions with our accounting advisors--both steps that Enron determined (and V&E accepted) would not be part of V&E's investigation. With the exception of Watkins, V&E spoke only with very senior people at Enron and Andersen. Those people, with few exceptions, had substantial professional and personal stakes in the matters under review.
context: Powers Report criticizes V&E's investigation methodology as structurally biased toward reaching favorable conclusions about the transactions.

label: Rhythms hedge compared to impossible commercial alternative
original_label: Rhythms hedge compared to impossible commercial alternative
quote: Due to the size and illiquidity of many of these investments, they could not practicably be hedged through traditional transactions with third parties. Fastow and Glisan developed a plan to hedge the Rhythms investment by taking advantage of the value in the Enron shares covered by the forward contracts.
context: Management implicitly justified the Rhythms structure by comparing it to an infeasible commercial alternative, suggesting it was the only option.

label: LJM2 compared as faster and cheaper buyer than third parties
original_label: LJM2 compared as faster and cheaper buyer than third parties

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Fastow presented participation as necessary to attract LJM investors
original_label: Fastow presented participation as necessary to attract LJM investors
quote: Fastow presented his participation as something he did not desire personally, but was necessary to attract investors to permit Enron to hedge its substantial investment in Rhythms NetConnections, Inc. ('Rhythms'), and possibly to purchase other assets in Enron's merchant portfolio.
context: Fastow framed his participation in LJM1 as serving Enron's business needs, not personal enrichment.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: LJM transactions presented as benefiting Enron shareholders
original_label: LJM transactions presented as benefiting Enron shareholders
quote: The Board apparently believed that the conflict, and the substantial risks associated with it, could be mitigated through certain controls (involving oversight by both the Board and Senior Management) to ensure that transactions were done on terms fair to Enron. In taking this step, the Board thought that the LJM partnerships would offer business benefits to Enron that would outweigh the potential costs.
context: Board approved the LJM partnerships based on Management's representation that they would benefit Enron and shareholders.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Skilling authorized Chewco to preserve JEDI partnership value
original_label: Skilling authorized Chewco to preserve JEDI partnership value
quote: Skilling told us that he was not surprised that Enron bought the interest back because personnel in Enron's Brazilian subsidiary had made misrepresentations to LJM1 in connection with the original sale, and that he would have authorized a buyback with any outside party under these circumstances.
context: Skilling justified the Cuiaba buyback as necessary to correct prior misrepresentations and preserve partnership value.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Raptor transactions justified as protecting merchant investments
original_label: Raptor transactions justified as protecting merchant investments
quote: In late 1999, at Skilling's urging, a group of Enron commercial and accounting professionals began to devise a mechanism that would allow Enron to hedge a portion of its merchant investment portfolio. These investments were 'marked to market,' with changes recorded in income every quarter for financial statement purposes. They had increased in value dramatically. Skilling said he wanted to protect the value of these investments and avoid excessive quarter-to-quarter volatility.
context: Skilling framed the Raptors as protecting Enron's business from market volatility, appealing to shareholder interests.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: PwC fairness opinion legitimates Rhythms transaction structure
original_label: PwC fairness opinion legitimates Rhythms transaction structure
quote: Enron obtained a fairness opinion from PricewaterhouseCoopers ('PwC') on the exchange of the 3.4 million restricted Enron shares for the Rhythms put and the $64 million note. PwC opined that the range of value for the Enron shares was $170-$223 million, that the range of value for the Rhythms put and note was $164-$204 million, and that the consideration received by Enron therefore was fair from a financial point of view.
context: Powers Report notes how the fairness opinion by a major accounting firm was invoked to legitimize the Rhythms structure.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Board oversight procedures invoked to justify conflict approval
original_label: Board oversight procedures invoked to justify conflict approval
quote: As we discuss further below, the Board required, and Management told the Board it was implementing, an ever-increasing set of procedures and controls over the related-party transactions. These included, most importantly, review and approval of all LJM transactions by Richard Causey, the Chief Accounting Officer; and Richard Buy, the Chief Risk Officer; and, later during the period, Jeffrey Skilling, the President and COO (and later CEO). The Board also directed its Audit and Compliance Committee to conduct annual reviews of all LJM transactions.
context: Powers Report describes how Management's representations about robust oversight procedures were used to justify the Board's approval of Fastow's conflict.

label: Derivatives, swaps and collars mask economic substance
original_label: Derivatives, swaps and collars mask economic substance
quote: Also during 2000, Enron engaged in other transactions with LJM2 intended to manage price and value risk with regard to certain merchant and similar assets by entering into derivatives, including swaps, puts, and collars. As part of such risk management transactions, LJM2 purchased equity interests in four structured finance vehicles for a total of approximately $127 million.
context: Powers Report quotes the 2001 proxy disclosure, which used sanitized financial terminology to describe what were actually loss-concealment vehicles.

label: Monetization terminology conceals asset sales
original_label: Monetization terminology conceals asset sales
quote: In the 10-Q for the second and third quarters of 1999, Enron described transactions with LJM that involved what it characterized as a pooling of loans and sales of securities representing rights to cash flow from the loans. These transactions also included direct or indirect investments by LJM in Enron affiliates. The effect on Enron's financial statements from these transactions varied. A monetization of a pool of Enron North America and Enron International assets.
context: Powers Report identifies how 'monetization' and technical financial language disguised what were sales of asset pools to related parties.

label: SPE structuring and non-consolidation requirements presented as technical matter
original_label: SPE structuring and non-consolidation requirements presented as technical matter
quote: Many of the transactions involve an accounting structure known as a 'special purpose entity' or 'special purpose vehicle' (referred to as an 'SPE' in this Summary and in the Report). A company that does business with an SPE may treat that SPE as if it were an independent, outside entity for accounting purposes if two conditions are met: (1) an owner independent of the company must make a substantive equity investment of at least 3% of the SPE's assets, and that 3% must remain at risk throughout the transaction; and (2) the independent owner must exercise control of the SPE.
context: Powers Report notes how the technical SPE rules were presented as neutral accounting requirements, obscuring their use as vehicles for off-balance-sheet accounting.

label: Credit capacity mathematics justified Raptor restructuring
original_label: Credit capacity mathematics justified Raptor restructuring
quote: By Enron's calculations, the restructuring allowed Enron to record only a $36.6 million credit reserve loss for the first quarter of 2001, rather than the $504 million loss Enron would have recorded if the Raptors had not been restructured.
context: Powers Report identifies how Enron accountants focused on the mathematical result of the restructuring to minimize the apparent impact.

label: Losses on merchant investments portrayed as temporary volatility
original_label: Losses on merchant investments portrayed as temporary volatility
quote: Skilling said he recalls being informed in only general terms that there was a credit capacity issue with the hedges in the Raptors due to the falling price of Enron stock and the assets being hedged, and that the problem could be solved. He told us he understood the matter to be an accounting issue, and that he recalls having no significant involvement in, or understanding of, the problem. Skilling also told us that, in his view, if it had been necessary to take a loss in the first quarter, Enron could have done so without undue harm to its stock price because many other companies at that time were reporting losses in high-tech investments.
context: Skilling characterized the Raptor credit crisis as merely an accounting adjustment that other companies were similarly experiencing.

label: Perfect profitability on LJM transactions minimized
original_label: Perfect profitability on LJM transactions minimized
quote: The LJM partnerships rarely lost money on a transaction with Enron that has been closed, so far as we are aware, even when they purchased assets that apparently declined in market value after the sale. These transactions had a significant effect on Enron's financial statements. Taken together, they resulted in substantial recognition of income, and the avoidance of substantial recognition of loss.
context: Powers Report notes the exceptional profitability of LJM on all transactions, suggesting systematic overpricing in LJM's favor.

label: Enron accountants directed structuring by Andersen advice
original_label: Enron accountants directed structuring by Andersen advice
quote: Accountants from Andersen were closely involved in structuring the Raptors. Attorneys from Vinson & Elkins also were consulted frequently, particularly on securities law issues, and also prepared the transaction documents.
context: Powers Report identifies how Management credited external professionals with structuring the Raptors, displacing responsibility for design flaws.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Enron changing industry, creating jobs, saving consumers money
original_label: Enron changing industry, creating jobs, saving consumers money
quote: During my time at Enron, I was immensely proud of what we accomplished. We believed that we were changing an industry, creating jobs, helping to resuscitate an ailing energy industry, and, by bringing choice to a monopoly dominated industry, we were trying to save consumers and small businesses billions of dollars each year. We believed fiercely in what we were doing.
context: Skilling's opening statement to Congress, justifying Enron's mission and his pride in the company's original purpose.

label: Board relied on outside auditors and accountants
original_label: Board relied on outside auditors and accountants
quote: Ours was a company that emphasized creativity but always in a manner that relied on the advice of the best people we could find, both those inside the company and the lawyers and accountants outside the company who advised us.
context: Skilling deflecting responsibility for transactions onto external advisors.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: I was not aware of inappropriate financing arrangements
original_label: I was not aware of inappropriate financing arrangements
quote: First, contrary to the refrain in the press, while I was at Enron I was not aware of any financing arrangements designed to conceal liabilities or inflate profitability.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: I did not dump stock; I held shares till August
original_label: I did not dump stock; I held shares till August
quote: Second, similarly, I did not dump any stock in Enron because I knew or even suspected that the company was in financial trouble. In fact, I left Enron holding about the same number of shares that I held at the beginning of 2001. On January 1, 2001, the start of my final year at Enron, I owned approximately 1.1 million shares of Enron stock. On August 14, the day I left, I owned about 940,000 shares of Enron stock.
context: Skilling denying knowledge of company's imminent collapse through his stock holdings claim.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Adequate controls in place; not my role to oversee
original_label: Adequate controls in place; not my role to oversee
quote: Third, with regard to the so-called LJM Partnerships, the Powers report criticizes me for supposedly not taking a more active role in reviewing the conflict of interest arising from the involvement in those partnerships of Enron's then CFO. context: Skilling claiming he met his limited obligations through existing controls.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Did not know transaction was designed to conceal losses
original_label: Did not know transaction was designed to conceal losses
quote: Fourth and finally, the Powers report also criticizes me for supposedly approving the restructuring of certain hedging transactions. The report then suggests that, If the account of other Enron employees is accurate, that transaction was designed to conceal losses on some of Enron's investments, and that I personally may have withheld information from the Board about that restructuring. I can state here today that I did not have any knowledge that the transaction was designated to conceal losses, and I did not do anything to withhold information from the Board of Directors of Enron Corporation.
context: Skilling denying knowledge of deceptive intent in transactions.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: SPEs commonplace; if properly established shift risk appropriately
original_label: SPEs commonplace; if properly established shift risk appropriately

label: Liquidity crisis, not fraud; company was solvent and profitable
original_label: Liquidity crisis, not fraud; company was solvent and profitable

At the time of Enron's collapse, the company was solvent, and the company was highly profitable, but apparently not liquid enough. That is my view of the principal cause of the failure.
context: Skilling minimizing the nature of Enron's collapse by recharacterizing it as a liquidity issue.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: I left believing company would be successful
original_label: I left believing company would be successful

label: Board entrusted us with controls; management failed to execute
original_label: Board entrusted us with controls; management failed to execute

The Special Committee concludes that the Audit Committee and the Board failed in their duties to oversee these transactions, and that we were insufficiently vigilant. I do not agree with that conclusion.

label: Arthur Andersen assured Board controls adequate and complied
original_label: Arthur Andersen assured Board controls adequate and complied
quote: The Audit Committee was repeatedly assured by senior management and by Arthur Andersen that these controls were being followed. The Board was told, and had every reason to believe, that Jeff Skilling, Enron's President and Chief Operating Officer at the time, Richard Causey, Enron's Chief Accounting Officer, Richard Buy, Enron's Chief Risk Officer, and Arthur Andersen, Enron's auditor, were ensuring that the Board's policies were followed and that any transactions with LJM were fair to Enron and properly accounted for.
context: Jaedicke citing repeated assurances from Arthur Andersen as basis for Board reliance.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Board did not know Kopper was involved in LJM
original_label: Board did not know Kopper was involved in LJM

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Board not told of other employees' investments in LJM
original_label: Board not told of other employees' investments in LJM

context: Jaedicke noting board's lack of knowledge about employee investments as concealment rather than board failure.

label: Board not told about asset sales and repurchases
original_label: Board not told about asset sales and repurchases

context: Jaedicke claiming board was not informed of churned transactions despite their suspicious timing.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Board not told about Raptor undercapitalization or restructuring
original_label: Board not told about Raptor undercapitalization or restructuring
quote: In early 2001, the Board was not told that the Raptor transactions were several hundred million dollars undercapitalized, or that management therefore intended to restructure those transactions requiring issuance of some 800 million additional shares of Enron stock.

label: Management and advisors never reported unfairness or violations to Board
original_label: Management and advisors never reported unfairness or violations to Board

context: Jaedicke explaining board relied on positive representations from those bound to report concerns.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Board cannot be faulted for information that was withheld or misrepresented
original_label: Board cannot be faulted for information that was withheld or misrepresented

context: Jaedicke using concealment of information to defend board against criticism.

label: Arthur Andersen failed professional responsibilities and audit obligations
original_label: Arthur Andersen failed professional responsibilities and audit obligations
quote: The evidence available to us suggests that Andersen did not fulfill its professional responsibilities in connection with its audits of Enron's financial statements, or its obligation to bring to the attention of Enron's Board (or the Audit or Compliance Committee) concerns about Enron's internal controls over the related-party transactions.
context: Jaedicke citing Arthur Andersen's failure as explanation for board's reliance.

label: Boards entitled to rely on outside consultants and auditor judgment
original_label: Boards entitled to rely on outside consultants and auditor judgment
quote: By necessity, Boards of Directors must rely—and the law allows them to rely—on outside advisers who are hired by the Board and owe their duties to the Board. As the Report found, Enron's Board of Directors reasonably relied on the professional judgment of Arthur Andersen concerning Enron's financial statements and the adequacy of internal controls. Andersen failed to meet its responsibility in both respects.
context: Jaedicke explaining board's legal entitlement to rely on external auditors.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Systemic failure due to employee dishonesty, not board negligence
original_label: Systemic failure due to employee dishonesty, not board negligence
quote: What happened at Enron has been described as a systemic failure. As it pertains to the Board, I see it instead as a cautionary reminder of the limits of a director's role. Our job as directors was necessarily limited by the nature of Enron's enterprise—which was worldwide in scope, employed more than 20,000 people, and engaged in a vast array of trading and development activities. By force of necessity, we could not know personally all of the employees. As we now know, key employees whom we thought we knew proved to be dishonest or disloyal.
context: Jaedicke attributing failure to employee dishonesty rather than board oversight deficiency.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Directors entitled to rely on honesty of subordinates until suspicion
original_label: Directors entitled to rely on honesty of subordinates until suspicion
quote: Directors are also, as the Report recognizes, entitled to rely on the honesty and integrity of their subordinates and advisers until something occurs to put them on suspicion that something is wrong. We did all of this, and more. Sadly, despite all that we tried to do, in the face of all the assurances we received, we had no cause for suspicion until it was too late.
context: Jaedicke defending board's reliance on subordinates' integrity as legal entitlement.

label: Winokur relied on information presented and advice of outside experts
original_label: Winokur relied on information presented and advice of outside experts
quote: We were required to do so on an informed basis, in good faith and in the honest belief that the actions we took were in the best interest of Enron. In reaching our decisions, we are entitled—and the Powers report concurs—to rely on the information we received from management and our outside experts, such as Arthur Andersen and Vinson & Elkins that we believed to be honest and reliable.
context: Winokur explaining board's reliance on management and expert presentations.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Directors cannot manage day-to-day; role is to direct and delegate
original_label: Directors cannot manage day-to-day; role is to direct and delegate
quote: The reality in the modern corporation is that directors cannot, and are not expected to, manage a company on a day to day basis. Rather, to be a director is to direct. We were required to do so on an informed basis, in good faith and in the honest belief that the actions we took were in the best interest of Enron. We then delegated to the company management and its outside advisors the responsibility to carry out our directions.
context: Winokur defining limited board role to justify delegation of responsibility.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Business decision evaluated on facts known at time; we acted in good faith
original_label: Business decision evaluated on facts known at time; we acted in good faith
quote: The Report makes clear that the directors were acting in good faith when they approved these transactions. It also recognizes that we as a Board held an honest belief that these transactions—although not without risk—were in the best interests of Enron's shareholders. The Report acknowledges that this was our independent business judgment, formed in consultation with outside experts from Arthur Andersen and Vinson Elkins, on which we were—and are—entitled to rely. With the benefit of hindsight, my colleagues on the Special Committee, without my participation, disagree with some of the decisions made by the Board, but they offer no suggestion that the Board did not act honestly and in good faith in approving these structures.
context: Winokur claiming good faith as defense against ex post facto criticism.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Raptor III transaction was not disclosed to Board
original_label: Raptor III transaction was not disclosed to Board
quote: The Report notes that a vehicle called Raptor III was created by Enron management, purportedly to hedge an investment in New Power stock. The Report makes clear that this transaction was never disclosed to the Board by anyone in management, although it was reviewed by Andersen. I cannot and will not defend this transaction.
context: Winokur conceding transaction was undisclosed but defending board from responsibility.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Raptor recapitalization concealed from Board; credit problems not disclosed
original_label: Raptor recapitalization concealed from Board; credit problems not disclosed
quote: The credit problems with the Raptor entities which began in late 2000 were not disclosed to the Board. The decision in early 2001 to recapitalize the Raptor structure with an $800 million forward contract on Enron stock was, likewise, concealed from us.
context: Winokur describing critical information kept from board.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Churned transactions concealed from Board
original_label: Churned transactions concealed from Board
quote: The Report notes that there was an observable pattern of assets being sold to LJM in one quarter, with earnings being booked, only to be repurchased by Enron in the following quarter. This, too, was concealed from the Board.
context: Winokur noting systematic concealment of suspicious transaction patterns.

label: Failure of character, not controls; everyone knew Board's requirements
original_label: Failure of character, not controls; everyone knew Board's requirements
quote: I attribute this to a failure not of controls, but of character. Everyone involved in these transactions—including Arthur Andersen, Vinson & Elkins, Andrew Fastow, Jeff Skilling, Rick Buy, Rick Causey and our internal legal counsel—knew that the Board had imposed extensive procedures to ensure that a critical overarching requirement would be met: Before any transaction could be approved, it had to be demonstrated that the transaction was on terms that were fair to Enron and negotiated at arms' length.
context: Winokur shifting blame to individual character rather than board governance.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: I cannot defend Raptor III; but oversight controls were ignored by those responsible
original_label: I cannot defend Raptor III; but oversight controls were ignored by those responsible

context: Winokur acknowledging unfairness but defending board by noting concealment.

label: LJM transactions described as hedges and monetizations, not earnings manipulation
original_label: LJM transactions described as hedges and monetizations, not earnings manipulation

context: Winokur citing sanitized technical language used to describe transactions.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: SPEs permitted by accounting rules if structured correctly; widely accepted practice
original_label: SPEs permitted by accounting rules if structured correctly; widely accepted practice
quote: I want to first address the current criticism directed at Enron's use of widely-accepted and well-established off balance sheet financing or special purpose vehicles to raise money. context: Jaedicke defending SPE usage as standard industry practice within accounting rules.

label: Other broadband companies also declined; not unique to Enron
original_label: Other broadband companies also declined; not unique to Enron

context: Winokur comparing Enron's business failures to industry-wide downturns.

label: Hedging described as managing P&L volatility and risk mitigation
original_label: Hedging described as managing P&L volatility and risk mitigation

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Rhythms restatement was accounting error, not improper hedge
original_label: Rhythms restatement was accounting error, not improper hedge
quote: It is also important, I believe, to point out that the restatement of $100 million in earnings from the Rhythms transaction is not the result of a hedge that didn't work. context: Winokur recharacterizing major earnings restatement as technical accounting mistake.

label: Fastow was CFO required to exercise fiduciary duty; Board oversight through controls
original_label: Fastow was CFO required to exercise fiduciary duty; Board oversight through controls
quote: In order to ensure that this duty was honored, Messrs. Skilling and Lay were given the authority to require Mr. Fastow to resign at any time from his involvement with LJM. Mr. Skilling also was charged with the responsibility to supervise Mr. Fastow's involvement, to make sure it did not become a disruption to the company and to ensure that his compensation from the LJM transactions was moderate. Mr. Skilling reported to us that he was discharging these obligations; it now appears that he did not do so.
context: Winokur noting board delegated oversight to Skilling, who failed to execute.

label: Management presented substantial benefits justifying LJM structure
original_label: Management presented substantial benefits justifying LJM structure
quote: As noted in the Report, LJM1 and LJM2 were presented to the Board as having significant benefits to Enron. Senior management discussed with the Board the very real and substantial benefits to Enron of such a structure.
context: Jaedicke explaining board reliance on management's presentation of benefits.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: McMahon did not know what happened after he was transferred
original_label: McMahon did not know what happened after he was transferred
quote: I found out when the Special Committee report came out last week. So you didn't find out the result of this until last week? No. I had moved out of the treasurer role apparently when——

label: Controls delegation to Causey and Buy
original_label: Controls delegation to Causey and Buy
quote: In October 1999, when the process was established for approval of transactions with LJM, the process is absolutely crystal clear. It involved approval by Mr. Causey and Mr. Buy.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Did not receive approval memo

original_label: LJM approval process involved multiple reviewers

original_label: Company was profitable despite losses

original_label: Structured arrangement for risk management

label: Compliance with established procedures and regulations
original_label: Compliance with established procedures and regulations
quote: We propose that the probable cause in the final report present the following causal factors to fully reflect the circumstances of this accident: uncommanded airplane-nose-down inputs from the MCAS due to erroneous AOA values and the flight crew's inadequate use of manual electric trim and management of thrust to maintain airplane control.
context: US accredited representative (NTSB, FAA, Boeing) shifts focus from MCAS system design failures to flight crew failure to follow procedures, implying that if crews had performed established procedures correctly, the accident would not have occurred.

label: Crew responsibility for inadequate response
original_label: Crew responsibility for inadequate response
quote: uncommanded airplane-nose-down inputs from the MCAS due to erroneous AOA values and the flight crew's inadequate use of manual electric trim and management of thrust to maintain airplane control.
context: US representatives characterize the accident cause by emphasizing crew 'inadequate use' rather than system design, framing the pilots as responsible parties.

label: Operator responsibility for crew preparation
original_label: Operator responsibility for crew preparation
