context: US representatives propose adding Ethiopian Airlines as a contributing cause, shifting focus from Boeing and FAA system design decisions to the airline's crew training failures.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: AOA sensor failure rather than design defect
original_label: AOA sensor failure rather than design defect
quote: Cause of the AOA erroneous data: Collins Aerospace, the manufacturer of the airplane's AOA sensor, was named as a technical advisor to the US team in April 2019 after the EAIB requested assistance investigating the most likely failure modes for the AOA sensor based on the accident data. Although the EAIB draft report acknowledges Collins' factual report, the EAIB draft report does not acknowledge Collins' fault tree analysis, which demonstrated that the recorded FDR data from the accident were not consistent with any internal failure of the AOA sensor; instead, those data were fully consistent with previous instances of partial AOA vane separation due to a bird strike.
context: US representatives argue that the erroneous AOA data resulted from external bird strike rather than sensor design defect, thereby displacing liability from Boeing's design to an external environmental cause.

label: Bird strike as sufficient external cause
original_label: Bird strike as sufficient external cause
quote: A bird weighing at least 0.5 pound (0.23 kilogram) impacting the vane at 170 knots (the estimated airspeed of the airplane at the time of the left AOA sensor performance deviation) would be sufficient to cause the vane to break at the hub and separate from the AOA sensor.
context: US representatives present evidence that a relatively small bird strike could cause the sensor failure, implying this is a normal external hazard rather than a system vulnerability.

label: Search timing and scope minimized
original_label: Search timing and scope minimized
quote: The EAIB draft report provides some details regarding a runway area search after the accident but inappropriately suggests that the lack of bird remains or AOA vane remnants indicates that the airplane was not impacted by a foreign object. The EAIB report fails to state that the search occurred 8 days after the accident and that the search did not include the area surrounding taxiway D, even though FDR data indicated that the airplane would have been positioned above the taxiway when the left AOA sensor data became erroneous.
context: US representatives reframe the negative findings of a search for bird remains, pointing to methodological deficiencies to maintain that a bird strike nonetheless occurred, minimizing the lack of physical evidence.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: MCAS design changes were officially approved
original_label: MCAS design changes were officially approved
quote: Boeing's changes to the MCAS design were official in March 2016 and were communicated to the FAA in July 2016, as described in the NTSB System Safety and Certification Specialist's Report, section H, Certification of the MCAS Implementation and Function. Boeing applied for and, in March 2017, was granted an amended type certificate for the 737-8 MAX.
context: US representatives assert that MCAS changes were formally approved by the FAA through established certification procedures, treating regulatory approval as settling the question of design adequacy.

label: Boeing provided bulletins to all operators
original_label: Boeing provided bulletins to all operators
quote: Boeing provided information to all 737 MAX operators in November 2018 (after the Lion Air accident but before the Ethiopian Airlines accident) to address uncommanded MCAS inputs. This information included operations manual bulletin (OMB)/FCOM bulletin ETH-12, FAA emergency AD 2018-23-51, a multi-operator message, dedicated meetings, and email messages.
context: US representatives emphasize that Boeing distributed procedural guidance to address MCAS problems, implying that operator and crew responsibility for understanding and implementing these procedures lay with the airlines.

label: Crew failure to follow established procedures
original_label: Crew failure to follow established procedures
quote: Flight crew performance played a critical role in the accident sequence; however, a discussion of the accident flight crew's performance (including CRM) was not sufficiently developed in the EAIB draft report, which continues to focus heavily on system design issues.
context: US representatives redirect accident causation toward crew performance rather than system design, framing pilots as critical decision-makers whose performance should be examined rather than system vulnerabilities.

label: Crew did not use proper procedures
original_label: Crew did not use proper procedures
quote: The EAIB report inaccurately states that the crew performed actions per the procedure. Evidence shows that the crew did not appropriately perform non-normal procedures after receiving annunciations relating to unreliable airspeed, stall warning, and runaway stabilizer. The crew also did not respond as expected to the overspeed warning by disconnecting the autothrottle and reducing power.
context: US representatives characterize the crew's actions as failures to follow procedure, repeatedly emphasizing what the crew should have done rather than system design failures.

label: Crew failure to use manual electric trim
original_label: Crew failure to use manual electric trim
quote: If the crew had conducted the procedure in the emergency AD and the FCOM bulletin, the crew would have used manual electric trim to reduce control forces. However, FDR data show minimal crew use of manual electric trim. If the crewmembers had performed the memory items for the airspeed unreliable and/or runaway stabilizer checklists, they would have disengaged the autothrottle. A manual reduction of thrust would have further assisted in reducing control forces. However, FDR data show that the autothrottle remained engaged and that thrust remained at full power.
context: US representatives repeatedly contrast established procedures with crew actions, framing multiple instances of crew non-compliance to demonstrate that the accident resulted from crew performance rather than system design.

label: Control remained possible with proper crew response
original_label: Control remained possible with proper crew response
quote: The EAIB draft report incorrectly states (in several places) that the MCAS made control of the airplane impossible but neglects to state that, if the crew had manually reduced thrust and appropriately used the manual electric trim, the airplane would have remained controllable despite uncommanded MCAS input.
context: US representatives minimize the severity of MCAS system failures by asserting that control remained available through alternative means, reframing system failure as a crew response problem.

label: Crew responsibility for understanding system interaction
original_label: Crew responsibility for understanding system interaction
quote: Even if such a reference document did not exist, the flight crew should have been trained on 737-8 MAX non-normal procedures. Because crew response to in-flight anomalies is time critical, these in-flight reference documents are not intended to provide flight crews with an in-depth understanding of a system before responding to an anomaly. Rather, non-normal procedures are designed to provide flight crews with information to diagnose and respond to a system-related issue in a timely manner based on observable flight deck effects.
context: US representatives argue that even absent explicit documentation, crews were responsible for understanding and executing non-normal procedures, displacing responsibility from Boeing for clear system documentation to crew training.

label: Crew failed to recognize and respond appropriately
original_label: Crew failed to recognize and respond appropriately
quote: Given that the conditions were met for the IAS DISAGREE and ALT DISAGREE messages to be annunciated to the crewmembers, their lack of conversation or action in response to the annunciations should be explored in the context of the flight deck environment, workload, crew experience, and training. The report's assumption that those messages did not appear, which is contrary to Boeing's description of the alerting system and the results of simulator testing during the investigation, severely limits the opportunity for recognizing and addressing potential crew training and experience improvements.
context: US representatives reframe the absence of recorded alerts as evidence that the crew should have recognized and responded to them, shifting focus to crew performance and training deficiencies.

label: Crew failed to notice autothrottle issue despite signals
original_label: Crew failed to notice autothrottle issue despite signals
quote: Because the autothrottle remained engaged and responsive to the erroneous AOA inputs, the autothrottle did not transition to N1 mode and remained in the ARM mode with takeoff thrust. The expected crew response is to manually control thrust in this situation; however, the lack of manual control and the absence of flight crew conversation regarding the thrust settings indicate that the crew did not notice the autothrottle's failure to transition to N1, even when the aural overspeed warning triggered as the airplane accelerated beyond about 340 knots.
context: US representatives emphasize crew failure to recognize and respond to system status changes despite available aural and visual warnings, framing this as a crew performance failure.

label: Airlines responsible for crew dissemination and understanding
original_label: Airlines responsible for crew dissemination and understanding
quote: The bulletin and emergency AD provided information to ensure that flight crews were aware of the possibility for repeated nose-down trim commands after an erroneously high single AOA sensor input and had specific guidance for recognizing the event and responding appropriately. Performance of the correct action depends on flight crews having access to, understanding, and applying the information presented in those documents. The report states that the bulletin and emergency AD were disseminated to Ethiopian Airlines flight crews via the logipad system, but the report does not discuss the effectiveness of this dissemination method or opportunities to improve crew access to, and understanding of, the disseminated information, which could benefit other operators that use a similar system to provide flight crews with critical information.
context: US representatives shift responsibility to Ethiopian Airlines for ensuring crew understanding and application of procedural bulletins, rather than examining whether Boeing's guidance was sufficiently clear or the system design itself was adequate.

label: CRM issues related to crew experience and authority
original_label: CRM issues related to crew experience and authority
quote: The CRM aspects not discussed in the report include, but are not limited to, the following: Division of duties, Operator CRM training, Expected/as-trained CRM performance, Flight deck communication, First officer's limited flight experience, Potential authority gradient
context: US representatives propose examining crew resource management issues including the first officer's limited experience and authority dynamics, implying crew-level factors contributed to the accident.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: System safety improvements to prevent future accidents
original_label: System safety improvements to prevent future accidents

The software updates include AOA signal monitoring (from both AOA sensors), MCAS activation and stabilizer resynchronization logic, maximum command limit, and flight deck alerting. These software enhancements provide additional functionality to prevent erroneous MCAS activation and ensure that sufficient maneuvering capability would be provided if multiple MCAS activations were to occur.
context: US representatives detail Boeing's post-accident safety improvements, implying the company acted responsibly to prevent future harm after learning from the accidents.

Neither the pilot-in-command nor the second-in-command can operate the 737 MAX unless they have completed the ground and flight training documented in this appendix.
context: US representatives highlight regulatory actions by the FAA that formalized new training requirements, treating formal compliance-based solutions as addressing the underlying safety issues.

original_label: Injuries trivial relative to use

original_label: Manufacturers report no accidents or injuries

original_label: Problem due to supplier's defective part

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Compliance with regulations settled the safety question
original_label: Compliance with regulations settled the safety question
quote: The FAA' s aircraft certification process has played a maj or role in producing airliners with an exemplary safety record consisting of a five-year worldwide average of only one fatal airliner crash for every 2 V2 to 3 million flights, and a U.S. record of only one airline passenger fatality in more than 10 years. Nonetheless, as with any system that is designed and operated by humans, the certification process can never be perfect, and the two tragic crashes that resulted in the creation of the JATR reveal a critical need to review the process to determine whether improvement and modernization are warranted.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance

To the extent they do not address every scenario, compliance with every applicable regulation and standard does not necessarily ensure safety.

label: FAA personnel approved derivative aircraft status without doubt

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement

original_label: MCAS described as fragmented among several documents

As a result, the MCAS description, including architecture, interfaces, logics, etc., is fragmented among several documents. Finding F4.2-B: Although MCAS may have been briefed to some FAA personnel, key aspects of the MCAS function such as intended function description, its interfaces, and architecture, were not directly visible to the FAA in a straightforward manner through the certification deliverable documents.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: FAA certification personnel not fully aware of MCAS details
original_label: FAA certification personnel not fully aware of MCAS details

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: MCAS design not highlighted as requiring special scrutiny
original_label: MCAS design not highlighted as requiring special scrutiny

context: The JATR observation documents that MCAS was not formally identified within Boeing or FAA processes as requiring heightened attention, diffusing responsibility for oversight.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: FHA and PSSA information submitted late, too late for FAA influence
original_label: FHA and PSSA information submitted late, too late for FAA influence
quote: Finding F4.3-A: The FAA certification process resulted in FHA/ PSSA information being submitted much too late (at type inspection authorization) for the FAA to have any influence on the proposed MCAS design for the purpose of demonstrating compliance. The FHA information that is delivered to the FAA is the FHA summary. Therefore, the FAA does not have the details of the analysis, which are documented in Boeing's internal coordination sheets (including important FHA assumptions). FAA's visibility into important system safety information was therefore incomplete and fragmented.
context: The JATR finding shows that Boeing's control over timing of safety analysis submissions and the FAA's receipt of only summaries, not details, diffused responsibility across organizational barriers.

label: FAA retained MCAS system safety documents then delegated to Boeing ODA
original_label: FAA retained MCAS system safety documents then delegated to Boeing ODA
quote: Finding F5.1-A: The FAA extensively delegated compliance findings on the B737-8 MAX project to the Boeing ODA. Safety critical areas, including system safety documents related to MCAS, were initially retained by the FAA and then delegated to the Boeing ODA.
context: The JATR finding documents the FAA's decision to transfer responsibility for MCAS safety assessment from its own staff to Boeing's designated authority.

label: FAA lacked capacity to review Boeing's massive certification work
original_label: FAA lacked capacity to review Boeing's massive certification work
quote: Observation O5.2-B: The Boeing ODA organization is staffed by approximately 1,500 people, whereas the FAA's BASOO is staffed by 45 people. Finding F5.2-A: There may be a lack of capacity and depth of experience of BASOO engineering members to approve and make findings of compliance for retained items. a) Out of 45 BASOO personnel, there are 18 working-level engineers and 6 senior engineers (24 engineers total). The JATR team was unable to conclusively determine the levels of experience of the working-level engineers and understands at least some of them may be entry-level engineers.
context: The JATR documentation shows that structural resource imbalance (1,500 Boeing staff versus 24 FAA engineers) created conditions where delegation of safety-critical functions became necessary, displacing responsibility to the manufacturer.

label: Pilot assumption that crew would take immediate corrective action
original_label: Pilot assumption that crew would take immediate corrective action
quote: To be consistent with §§ 25.671 and 25.672, and to comply with the guidance in AC 25-7C, Boeing utilized four fundamental assumptions on crew actions in the flight control FHA for the B737 MAX and other Boeing models. The third assumption, taken from AC 25-7C, stated: The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate high control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Finding F9.3-A: Based on the JATR team's review of preliminary accident information, in both aircraft accidents the flight crew did not appear to meet the immediate action assumption.
context: Boeing's design and certification relied on assumptions about pilot behavior that proved false in both accidents, yet the assumption framed pilot failure as the mitigation rather than design failure.

label: Pilot recognition time assumptions did not account for surprise or complexity
original_label: Pilot recognition time assumptions did not account for surprise or complexity
quote: Observation O2.8-C: Although the above guidance is aimed at test pilots conducting test flights, applicants seem to use this guidance as a design assumption that the pilot will be able to respond correctly within 4 seconds of the occurrence of a malfunction. For example, in the case of the B737 MAX, it was assumed that, since MCAS activation rate is 0.27 degrees of horizontal stabilizer movement per second, during the 4 seconds that it would take a pilot to respond to an erroneous activation, the stabilizer will only move a little over 1 degree, which should not create a problem for the pilot to overcome.
context: The JATR observation documents that Boeing's design embedded assumptions about pilot response times that were never validated against actual pilot behavior in complex operational environments.

label: Assumption that MAX pilots experienced with NG would easily adapt
original_label: Assumption that MAX pilots experienced with NG would easily adapt

These approaches were driven by Boeing's assumptions that the MAX is a replacement for the NG and that MAX pilots will be experienced NG pilots. These assumptions were not warranted, as demonstrated by airlines for which the MAX was the first B737 model to be purchased (e.g., Air Canada), and by new pilots entering service directly to the MAX (e.g., the First Officer on ET302).
context: The JATR finding documents that Boeing's certification basis rested on unvalidated assumptions about pilot experience that proved false in actual operations, yet these assumptions justified design exceptions.

label: MCAS stabilizer movement assumed too small for pilot difficulty

quote: Observation O2.8-C: Although the above guidance is aimed at test pilots conducting test flights, applicants seem to use this guidance as a design assumption that the pilot will be able to respond correctly within 4 seconds of the occurrence of a malfunction. For example, in the case of the B737 MAX, it was assumed that, since MCAS activation rate is 0.27 degrees of horizontal stabilizer movement per second, during the 4 seconds that it would take a pilot to respond to an erroneous activation, the stabilizer will only move a little over 1 degree, which should not create a problem for the pilot to overcome.
context: Boeing's design rationale minimized the harm from unintended MCAS activation by arguing the physical effect would be too small to overcome, contradicting accident evidence.

label: Multiple MCAS activations not worse than single activation
original_label: Multiple MCAS activations not worse than single activation

context: The JATR observation documents that Boeing minimized the risk of cascading MCAS failures by assuming crews would successfully counter each one, contradicting what actually occurred in the accidents.

label: Worst-case AOA failure scenario already catastrophic so not reassessed
original_label: Worst-case AOA failure scenario already catastrophic so not reassessed
quote: Observation O6.9-A: As far as AOA failures are concerned, the JATR team observed that the S&MF analysis was limited to a single worst-case scenario: loss of AOA on one side plus erroneous AOA on the other side. Other AOA failures were not evaluated because the worst-case failure modes were analyzed and the hazard analyses in the S&MF was limited to only those combined worst-case failures. Because this worst-case scenario was already considered catastrophic, the S&MF analysis was not updated after introduction of MCAS.
context: The JATR observation documents that Boeing's safety analysis stopped after identifying one worst-case scenario, treating that as sufficient even though MCAS introduced new failure interactions.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance

original_label: MCAS design assumed compliance with regulations satisfied safety

original_label: Boeing compliance with certification basis satisfied regulatory requirement

label: MCAS presented as stability augmentation system for pitch characteristics

Collectively, the changes incorporated into the B737 MAX design resulted in increased fuel efficiency, increased range, and a reduced noise profile compared to its predecessor, the B737 NG.
context: The JATR background section introduces MCAS in neutral technical language as a normal feature alongside efficiency improvements, obscuring its novel use of the trim system and safety-critical role.

label: MCAS function described without revealing continuous automatic operation
original_label: MCAS function described without revealing continuous automatic operation

label: Speed trim system function called MCAS without distinguishing purposes
original_label: Speed trim system function called MCAS without distinguishing purposes

context: The JATR findings document that MCAS was extended from high-speed pitch control to low-speed stall prevention without formally recognizing this as creating a novel dual-purpose system, masking the functional expansion.

original_label: Fragmented SSA and FHA called normal certification documentation practice

label: Guidelines and criteria for substantial change vague and subject to interpretation

label: FAA official disagreement about interpretation of Changed Product Rule

label: AC 25.1302-1 insufficient to emphasize human factors integration
original_label: AC 25.1302-1 insufficient to emphasize human factors integration

context: The JATR observation identifies inadequacy in FAA guidance materials themselves rather than in how Boeing applied them, shifting blame from the applicant to the regulatory authority.

label: AC 25-7D and 25.1329-1C pilot recognition time guidance not substantiated
original_label: AC 25-7D and 25.1329-1C pilot recognition time guidance not substantiated
quote: Observation O2.8-D: No studies were found that substantiate the FAA guidance concerning pilot recognition time and pilot reaction time. Observation O2.8-E: Several FAA studies with general aviation pilots demonstrate that these general aviation pilots may take many seconds, and in some cases many minutes, to recognize and respond to malfunctions (e.g., DOT/FAA/AM-97/24; DOT/FAA/AM-02/19; DOT/FAA/AM-05/23).
context: The JATR observations critique the FAA's own guidance as lacking scientific foundation and contradicted by the FAA's own research, implicitly questioning the FAA's competence in setting the standard Boeing relied upon.

label: FAA guidance on pilot reaction time based on decades-old autopilot practice
original_label: FAA guidance on pilot reaction time based on decades-old autopilot practice
quote: Finding F2.8-D: The 3-second reaction time assumption dates back decades, to where the performance of the autopilot was constantly monitored by the crew in flight (e.g., guidance given in AC 25.1329-1A, Automatic Pilot Systems Approval, dated July 8, 1968). However, with increasing reliability and advances in flight deck alerting and displays, it may no longer be appropriate to assume that the pilot flying will be monitoring the automation as closely as in the past.
context: The JATR finding documents that the FAA's guidance was based on 50-year-old assumptions about pilot behavior that may no longer apply, implicitly critiquing FAA guidance as outdated.

label: FAA lacked sufficient human factors expertise on certification staff
original_label: FAA lacked sufficient human factors expertise on certification staff
quote: While issues in human-machine interaction are at the core of all recent aviation accidents and are implicated in the two B737 MAX accidents, the FAA has very few human factors and human system integration experts on its certification staff.
context: The JATR finding identifies systemic inadequacy in FAA staffing and expertise, implicitly criticizing the regulatory authority for failing to maintain necessary technical competence.

label: MCAS not identified as novel despite previous use on military tanker
original_label: MCAS not identified as novel despite previous use on military tanker
quote: Observation O6.9-B: Boeing engineers did not see MCAS as new or novel, partly because it was already operational on the military tanker version of the B767. Observation O6.9-C: Boeing conducted an S&MF analysis on Revision C of the STS requirements for MCAS software, which only included high-speed values in its lookup table (as was used in the military tanker version of the B767). Observation O6.9-D: During Boeing flight tests, the company added low-speed values to the MCAS lookup table in its Revision D of the STS requirements for MCAS.
context: The JATR observations document that Boeing treated MCAS as not novel because of prior military use, thereby not updating safety analyses when the civilian application was extended to low-speed flight.

label: Safety analysis not updated beyond MCAS Revision C despite low-speed extension
original_label: Safety analysis not updated beyond MCAS Revision C despite low-speed extension
quote: Observation O6.9-F: The SSA was not updated beyond Revision C of the STS requirements for MCAS. The JATR team observed no documented risk, failure, or safety analyses conducted on the MCAS software beyond Revision C. Observation O6.9-G: Boeing determined the high-speed regime to be the critical aspect of MCAS, and thus no revision to the SSA was necessary when the low speeds were added to the software's lookup table.
context: The JATR observations document that Boeing explicitly decided not to update safety analyses when MCAS was functionally expanded, treating the original high-speed analysis as sufficient for the new low-speed capability.

label: Boeing made certification assumptions about pilot behavior unvalidated
original_label: Boeing made certification assumptions about pilot behavior unvalidated
quote: To be consistent with §§ 25.671 and 25.672, and to comply with the guidance in AC 25-7C, Boeing utilized four fundamental assumptions on crew actions in the flight control FHA for the B737 MAX and other Boeing models. The third assumption, taken from AC 25-7C, stated: The pilot will take immediate action to reduce or eliminate high control forces by re-trimming or changing configuration or flight conditions. Finding F9.3-A: Based on the JATR team's review of preliminary accident information, in both aircraft accidents the flight crew did not appear to meet the immediate action assumption. This assumption makes no allowance for differing training and certification requirements for flight crew operating under other CAAs.
context: The JATR finding documents that Boeing relied on regulatory guidance to justify design assumptions about pilot behavior that proved false, shifting responsibility to the guidance itself.

label: Changed product rule process described as effective for discrete changes
original_label: Changed product rule process described as effective for discrete changes

label: FAA approved the differences training determination
original_label: FAA approved the differences training determination
quote: Based on Boeing's misleading statements, half-truths, and omissions to the FAA AEG about MCAS, and in reliance on those statements and omissions, the FAA AEG agreed to delete all information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report.
context: Statement of Facts describing how Boeing obtained the FAA's Level B determination by concealing MCAS's expanded operational scope, framing the decision as the FAA's own.

label: Level B training versus Level D training cost framing
original_label: Level B training versus Level D training cost framing
quote: As Boeing knew, 'Level B' differences training was significantly less expensive for airlines to complete than 'Level D.' For example, a pilot could complete 'Level B' differences training from anywhere in the world in a matter of hours using a computer or tablet. In contrast, a pilot could complete 'Level D' differences training only by appearing in person wherever the pilot's airline operated a full-flight simulator. Apart from the cost of acquiring one or more multimillion-dollar simulators and other related expenses, airlines that were required by the FAA AEG to train pilots on a full-flight simulator could also lose revenue that the pilot might otherwise have generated from flying airline passengers during that time.
context: Statement of Facts explaining Boeing's financial motivation to secure Level B training, using technical training designations to obscure the economic stakes and safety implications.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Level B achievement as company success milestone
original_label: Level B achievement as company success milestone
quote: On or about August 16, 2016, before the FAA AEG published the 737 MAX FSB Report, the FAA AEG issued a provisional 'Level B' differences-training determination for the 737 MAX. At the time of this provisional determination, the FAA AEG was unaware that Boeing had expanded MCAS's operational scope. On or about the same day, Boeing Employee-1 recognized Boeing's achievement in an email to Boeing employees, including Boeing Employee-2, and wrote that the FAA AEG's provisional determination 'culminates more than 3 years of tireless and collaborative efforts across many business units' and that the 737 MAX program management 'is VERY happy.'
context: Statement of Facts showing Boeing Employee-1 framing the Level B determination as a company achievement earned through collaborative effort, obscuring the deception involved.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Boeing Employee-2 denies knowledge of expanded MCAS scope
original_label: Boeing Employee-2 denies knowledge of expanded MCAS scope
quote: Also, in and around the same time, Boeing Employee-2 caused Boeing to present a false and misleading presentation to the FAA AEG about MCAS. Boeing investigated, among other things, what information Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 provided to the FAA AEG about MCAS. In connection with this investigation, Boeing Employee-2 caused Boeing to represent in a presentation to the FAA AEG that, during the training-evaluation process, Boeing and the FAA AEG had 'discussed and agreed on [the] removal of MCAS' from the 737 MAX FSB Report and associated materials. This representation was misleading because Boeing Employee-2 had failed to disclose the 'shocker alert' chat communication and the fact that the FAA AEG was deprived of relevant information about MCAS. Following the Lion Air crash, Boeing Employee-2 told FAA AEG Employee-1 that he was previously unaware of MCAS's expanded operational scope and otherwise misled FAA AEG Employee-1 about Boeing Employee-2's prior knowledge of MCAS.
context: Statement of Facts describing Boeing Employee-2's post-crash attempt to deny prior knowledge of MCAS's expanded scope, despite the 'shocker alert' chat exchange.

label: MCAS described as limited to certification maneuver

quote: To fix this pitch-up characteristic, Boeing created MCAS and incorporated it as a part of the 737 MAX's flight controls. As originally designed, MCAS could only activate during a high-speed, wind-up turn.
context: Statement of Facts describing how Boeing initially characterized MCAS to the FAA AEG as limited in operational scope, minimizing its risk profile.

label: Responsibility resting on FAA's provisional determination
original_label: Responsibility resting on FAA's provisional determination
quote: On or about August 16, 2016, before the FAA AEG published the 737 MAX FSB Report, the FAA AEG issued a provisional 'Level B' differences-training determination for the 737 MAX. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 also understood, as Boeing Employee-1 acknowledged in his email on or about August 16, 2016, that the FAA AEG's 'Level B' differences determination for the 737 MAX was only a 'provisional approval [. . .] assuming no significant systems changes to the airplane.'
context: Statement of Facts framing the FAA's Level B determination as provisional and contingent, implicitly attributing responsibility for verification to the FAA.

original_label: Concealment of MCAS framed as keeping regulatory scope limited

This is what we sold to the regulators who have already granted us the Level B differences determination. To go back to them now, and tell them there is in fact a difference [. . .] would be a huge threat to that differences training determination.'
context: Statement of Facts showing Boeing Employee-1 using bureaucratic language ('Program Directives,' 'not create any differences') to frame concealment as adherence to policy.

original_label: Boeing Employee-1 denies intentional deception to regulators

On or about that same day, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 discussed MCAS in an internal Boeing electronic chat communication, writing in part: Boeing Employee-1: Oh shocker alerT! [sic] / MCAS is now active down to [Mach] .2 / It's running rampant in the sim on me / at least that's what [a Boeing simulator engineer] thinks is happening Boeing Employee-2: Oh great, that means we have to update the speed trim description in vol 2 Boeing Employee-1: so I basically lied to the regulators (unknowingly) Boeing Employee-2: it wasn't a lie, no one told us that was the case
