label: Pilot responsibility framing in crash analysis
original_label: Pilot responsibility framing in crash analysis
quote: Although Boeing knew about manufacturing, quality, safety, and anti-fraud risks capable of undermining the completeness, accuracy, and truthfulness of those records, Boeing did not implement additional or sufficient controls concerning the risk that its certifications of airworthiness to the FAA could be incomplete, inaccurate, false and/or fraudulent and that aircraft delivered to its customers 'conforms to its type design and is in a condition for safe operation.'
context: Factual Basis for Breach indicating Boeing's knowledge of risks but deflection of responsibility through framing of aircraft as conforming to design without addressing pilot training deficits.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Production efficiency prioritized over manufacturing quality
original_label: Production efficiency prioritized over manufacturing quality
quote: Between 2021 and 2023, Boeing conducted several Safety Risk Management assessments that identified out-of-sequence work as a risk factor that could cause the delivery of an 'unairworthy' or non-conforming aircraft to Boeing's customers. Despite the acknowledgement of this risk, the Safety Risk Management assessments did not sufficiently consider measures to reduce out-of-sequence work. Boeing senior executives prioritized the movement of aircraft through Boeing's factories over reducing out-of-sequence work to ensure production quality.
context: Factual Basis for Breach showing management's choice to prioritize production velocity as a competing business objective justifying acceptance of known manufacturing risk.

label: Compliance function excluded from safety risk assessments
original_label: Compliance function excluded from safety risk assessments
quote: Moreover, although fraud is an inherent risk in production and quality compliance activities, Boeing's Safety Risk Management assessments also failed to identify out-of-sequence risk as a fraud risk or consider enhanced production procedures, or preventive or detective controls, to mitigate the risk. Boeing's Global Compliance function, which is responsible for Boeing's anti-fraud ethics and compliance program, was not involved in the Safety Risk Assessments. Compliance therefore did not evaluate fraud risks associated with out-of-sequence work, including the risk of incomplete, inaccurate, false, and/or fraudulent statements to the FAA.
context: Factual Basis for Breach showing how separation of compliance from safety assessments dispersed responsibility for fraud detection.

label: False stamping framed as employee misunderstanding
original_label: False stamping framed as employee misunderstanding
quote: In or around April 2024, Boeing disclosed to the Fraud Section false stamping during the DPA term at the Boeing 787 manufacturing facility in Charleston, South Carolina. The false stamps caused Boeing's quality management systems to reflect that all required steps were complete, when they were not. Employees involved in the false stamping did not understand Boeing's stamping policy, were not familiar with its requirements, and were not effectively trained on it.
context: Factual Basis for Breach showing Boeing's characterization of false stamping as a training gap rather than a systemic fraud risk.

label: Stamping integrity and record completeness as technical policy matters
original_label: Stamping integrity and record completeness as technical policy matters
quote: Boeing received hundreds of reports of stamping non-compliance through its internal reporting channels. Boeing Compliance identified this anti-fraud risk during the DPA term and issued training and communications throughout the Company in response to the risk. Despite awareness of stamping non-compliance reports, Boeing did not conduct sufficient testing to evaluate whether its stamping integrity communications and training efforts were effective in practice and stamping issues persisted.
context: Factual Basis for Breach using technical terminology ('stamping integrity,' 'non-compliance reports') to describe a fraud risk that was not adequately tested or remediated.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Removal records policy treated as sufficient control
original_label: Removal records policy treated as sufficient control
quote: Boeing's airworthiness certifications to the FAA rely on the completeness and accuracy of Boeing's build records and the effectiveness of related manufacturing and quality processes. If installed parts are later removed during manufacturing, Boeing policy requires Boeing employees to document the removal in certain written records. The creation of a removal record initiates a process to ensure proper reinstallation of the part and record the individuals involved in removal, reinstallation, and reinspection. If a removal record was not completely resolved in Boeing's computer systems, including reinstallation and reinspection, a Boeing employee would not certify an aircraft as airworthy to the FAA.
context: Factual Basis for Breach describing Boeing's policy on removal records as if its existence constituted adequate control, despite known non-compliance.

label: Manufacturing and quality risks minimized as known but manageable
original_label: Manufacturing and quality risks minimized as known but manageable
quote: Although Boeing knew about manufacturing, quality, safety, and anti-fraud risks capable of undermining the completeness, accuracy, and truthfulness of those records, Boeing did not implement additional or sufficient controls concerning the risk that its certifications of airworthiness to the FAA could be incomplete, inaccurate, false and/or fraudulent and that aircraft delivered to its customers 'conform[] to its type design and is in a condition for safe operation,' in violation of the compliance program standards required by DPA Attachment C, including Paragraphs 3, 4, and 5.
context: Factual Basis for Breach characterizing known manufacturing and quality risks as acknowledged but not requiring enhanced anti-fraud controls.

label: Concealment of MCAS scope change phrased as regulatory discussion
original_label: Concealment of MCAS scope change phrased as regulatory discussion
quote: Shortly after the simulated test flight described in paragraph 30, Boeing Employee-1 talked with FAA AEG Employee-1, who asked Boeing Employee-1 about the simulated test flight. Boeing Employee-1 intentionally withheld and concealed from FAA AEG Employee-1 the fact that MCAS's operational scope had been expanded beyond what the FAA AEG relied upon when it issued its provisional 'Level B' differences-training determination for the 737 MAX.
context: Statement of Facts describing active concealment as simply 'talking with' the FAA AEG employee, using euphemistic phrasing to frame deliberate omission.

label: FAA AEG responsibility for accepting proposal to delete MCAS
original_label: FAA AEG responsibility for accepting proposal to delete MCAS
quote: On or about November 22, 2016, the other Boeing employee emailed the draft 737 MAX FSB Report back to the FAA AEG with proposed edits. Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 were included on this email. Boeing Employee-1 included a proposed edit to delete a reference to MCAS, and wrote, 'We agreed not to reference MCAS since it's outside normal operating envelope.' Neither Boeing Employee-1 nor Boeing Employee-2 shared the fact of MCAS's expanded operational scope with the FAA AEG or otherwise corrected the FAA AEG's misimpression that MCAS's operational scope was limited to high-speed, wind-up turns. In doing so, Boeing Employee-1 and Boeing Employee-2 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially 'agreed' to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same.
context: Statement of Facts showing Boeing Employee-1 using 'we agreed' language to frame the deletion of MCAS as a joint FAA-Boeing decision, obscuring the concealment.

label: Removal of MCAS information framed as regulatory agreement
original_label: Removal of MCAS information framed as regulatory agreement
quote: On or about January 17, 2017, Boeing Employee-1 again reminded the FAA AEG in an email to delete any reference to MCAS from the forthcoming 737 MAX FSB Report, and wrote, 'Flight Controls: Delete MCAS, recall we decided we weren't going to cover it [. . .] since it's way outside the normal operating envelope.' Again, Boeing Employee-1 deceived the FAA AEG into believing that the basis upon which the FAA AEG had initially 'decided' to remove any information about MCAS from the 737 MAX FSB Report—that MCAS could only activate during the limited operational scope of a high-speed, wind-up turn—remained the same.
context: Statement of Facts showing Boeing Employee-1 using 'we decided' and 'recall' to reframe concealment as pre-existing regulatory consensus.

label: FAA conducted independent review and testing
original_label: FAA conducted independent review and testing
quote: The FAA engaged with Boeing, operators, international civil aviation regulators, and independent review panels investigating the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302. This work resulted in the identification of seven safety issues that played a role in the two accidents.
context: FAA timeline document describes how independent expert bodies identified safety issues, implicitly situating the FAA as the authority responsible for determining what was wrong and fixing it.

label: FAA conducted comprehensive testing and certification
original_label: FAA conducted comprehensive testing and certification
quote: Multiple tests of software for failure conditions were conducted after Boeing submitted a new software architecture that relied on the simultaneous use of two Flight Control Computers. Initial testing was completed in November 2019, and the final evaluation was completed on August 13, 2020. Crew Workload/Human Factors 1302 testing with flight crews from Southwest Airlines, American Airlines, United Airlines, and Aeromexico was conducted during the week of December 2, 2019. Audit of the software development process was completed to verify safety requirements were appropriately coded into the software. The FAA completed an initial audit during the week of June 15, 2020, and the final audit on September 14, 2020. The FAA and Boeing conducted the certification flight test to evaluate Boeing's proposed changes to the automated flight control system on the 737 MAX during the week of June 29, 2020. All conditions flown were satisfactory.
context: FAA timeline enumerates multiple independent testing and verification activities conducted by the FAA, positioning regulatory agency approval as the mechanism that certified safety.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: FAA finding of compliance with applicable regulations
original_label: FAA finding of compliance with applicable regulations
quote: Boeing submitted its final design documentation to the FAA on October 16, 2020. The FAA reviewed the documentation, made a finding of compliance with the applicable regulations, and issued the design approval to Boeing on November 17, 2020.
context: FAA timeline describes the regulatory approval process culminating in a formal finding of compliance, treating regulatory sign-off as the decisive validation.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Airworthiness Directive mandates corrective actions
original_label: Airworthiness Directive mandates corrective actions
quote: The FAA issued an Airworthiness Directive on November 18, 2020, which applies to 737 MAX airplanes that received FAA airworthiness certificates and export certificates of airworthiness prior to the date of issuance of the Rescission of Emergency Order of Prohibition (November 18, 2020). The AD mandates actions to correct the unsafe condition.
context: FAA timeline presents issuance of Airworthiness Directive as the formal legal mechanism through which unsafe conditions are remedied.

label: Independent expert review commissions validate corrective measures
original_label: Independent expert review commissions validate corrective measures
quote: The FAA commissioned a TAB to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB is made up of experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX, including members from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the United States Air Force, the Volpe National Transportation Systems Center, and the FAA. The TAB originally met in Spring 2019 and reviewed proposed MCAS changes at that time. Since that time, they reviewed all proposed modifications and made recommendations throughout the process. The FAA addressed all return to service recommendations prior to rescinding the grounding order. The TAB delivered its final report to the FAA on November 17, 2020.
context: FAA timeline describes independent expert review process, positioning outside authorities as validators of the aircraft's safety and the FAA as the entity implementing their recommendations.

label: Joint international authorities review and approve return to service
original_label: Joint international authorities review and approve return to service
quote: The FAA established the JATR to conduct a review of the FAA's certification of the automated flight control system of the 737 MAX, determine compliance with all applicable regulations, and identify any future enhancements that may be necessary. The JATR was chaired by former NTSB Chairman Christopher Hart and included technical experts in a variety of disciplines from the FAA, NASA, and the civil aviation authorities of Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates. The JATR concluded its work and submitted its recommendations on October 11, 2019. The FAA addressed all recommendations that applied to the 737 MAX prior to approving the aircraft for return to service.
context: FAA timeline documents an international joint review process with expert technical authorities, distributing oversight responsibility across multiple governments and agencies.

label: Special Committee and DOT OIG conduct independent audits
original_label: Special Committee and DOT OIG conduct independent audits
quote: On March 25, 2019, Secretary Elaine L. Chao established a Special Committee to review the FAA's Aircraft Certification Process. It was co-chaired by Air Force General (Ret.) Darren McDew, former head of the U.S. Transportation Command, and Captain Lee Moak, former President of the Air Line Pilots Association. The Official Report of the Special Committee to Review the Federal Aviation Administration's Aircraft Certification Process was delivered to the Secretary on January 16, 2020. On March 19, 2019, Secretary Chao directed the DOT OIG to conduct an audit to compile an objective and detailed factual history of the activities that resulted in the certification of the Boeing 737 MAX.
context: FAA timeline documents establishment of independent oversight bodies by Cabinet-level officials, positioning high-level government audits as the mechanism ensuring accountability.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Certification demonstrates safety and meets standards
original_label: Certification demonstrates safety and meets standards
quote: The FAA's intent is to assure the global community that the 737 MAX is safe to operate and meets FAA certification standards.
context: FAA statement in executive summary asserting that meeting certification standards is equivalent to being safe for operation.

label: FAA retained all compliance findings and approvals
original_label: FAA retained all compliance findings and approvals
quote: During its evaluation of Boeing's proposed modifications, the FAA retained all compliance findings and approvals associated with the design changes related to MCAS. This thorough review has taken more than 22 months and included the full-time work of more than 40 engineers, inspectors, pilots, and technical support staff. The effort represents more than 60,000 FAA hours of review, certification testing, and evaluation of pertinent documents.
context: FAA executive summary emphasizing its direct oversight and extensive review effort to assure the public that proper authority reviewed all changes.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Compliance with regulations settles the matter
original_label: Compliance with regulations settles the matter
quote: As the State of Design agent, the FAA is providing this report to all States of Registry and to the general public to explain how the agency identified and addressed the safety issues affecting the 737 MAX. The FAA's intent is to assure the global community that the 737 MAX is safe to operate and meets FAA certification standards.
context: FAA framing in executive summary that meeting certification standards constitutes assurance of safety.

label: Design philosophy made system more robust
original_label: Design philosophy made system more robust
quote: The MCAS-related FCC software update is not applicable to the 737 NG because the 737 NG does not include MCAS and is therefore not included in the FAA certification efforts in this matter. However, Boeing will also review ancillary changes that can enhance the 737 NG. The FAA will work with Boeing to ensure that any issues related to the 737 MAX design change that may apply to the 737 NG will be addressed as applicable. Rather, and most importantly, MCAS enhances the earlier design philosophy to be more robust.
context: FAA characterization of MCAS as an enhancement that made the design more robust, minimizing the severity of the system that caused two fatal accidents.

label: Boeing responsible for design decisions and compliance
original_label: Boeing responsible for design decisions and compliance
quote: The aircraft manufacturer is responsible for making design decisions and showing compliance to applicable regulations. In this case, Boeing elected to include an additional flight control law in the STS, which is part of the flight control software that provides required control force feel to the pilot.
context: FAA description placing responsibility on Boeing for choosing to include MCAS in the design.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Without MCAS aircraft cannot meet regulatory requirements
original_label: Without MCAS aircraft cannot meet regulatory requirements
quote: Without MCAS, the 737 MAX would not meet FAA's regulatory requirements. Boeing proposed multiple updates to the MCAS function to address Safety Item #1: USE OF SINGLE ANGLE OF ATTACK (AOA) SENSOR, Safety Item #2: MCAS RESET GENERATES REPETITIVE MCAS COMMAND and Safety item #3: MCAS TRIM AUTHORITY in the previous chart.
context: FAA statement treating regulatory compliance as necessitating the existence of MCAS, thus justifying its inclusion in the original design.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Boeing developed all substantiating data under FAA oversight
original_label: Boeing developed all substantiating data under FAA oversight
quote: NOTE: Unless noted otherwise and in accordance with FAA rules (see 14 CFR 21.21) and policy (see FAA Order 8110.4c, paragraph 2-6.(j)(2)) Boeing developed all data (also known as substantiating data) and conducted all analysis and tests that are referenced in this report. The FAA oversees the process, reviews select substantiating data and may repeat any or all testing that the applicant conducts.
context: FAA disclaimer establishing that Boeing, not FAA, developed the technical evidence, while FAA only oversaw and selected what to review.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Design changes comply with existing certification basis
original_label: Design changes comply with existing certification basis
quote: The MCAS was designed and certified for the 737 MAX to enhance the pitch stability of the airplane. As such, the design change is neither substantial (the change in design is not so extensive to require a complete investigation of compliance) nor significant (there was no change to the general configuration or the assumptions used for certification) from a product-level-change point of view. Rather, and most importantly, MCAS enhances the earlier design philosophy to be more robust. Therefore Boeing was required to demonstrate compliance with the existing 737 MAX Certification Basis.
context: FAA technical characterization of MCAS modifications as non-substantial changes requiring only compliance with existing certification basis, not fresh review.

label: Flightcrews unable to manage alerts and procedures
original_label: Flightcrews unable to manage alerts and procedures
quote: FDR data from both accidents show that the flightcrews were unable to effectively manage the stabilizer movement and multiple flight deck effects that resulted from the single AOA sensor failure.
context: FAA summary of accident findings framing the problem as pilot failure to manage rather than design failure to protect.

label: Crew workload is responsibility of operators and training
original_label: Crew workload is responsibility of operators and training
quote: The FAA conclusion from this analysis indicated that an average crew with no prior awareness could sort out the failure scenario and could correctly mitigate the failure using existing procedures.
context: FAA assessment that existing procedures were sufficient, placing responsibility on pilots to execute them rather than on design to prevent the problem.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Service information approved and complies with regulations
original_label: Service information approved and complies with regulations
quote: The FAA reviewed and approved the service information (service bulletins) Boeing submitted that contain the design changes that address the unsafe condition and other issues relevant to the matters discussed in this report. The agency has completed review and approved the following service information: Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737 22A1342 RB, dated November 17, 2020, describes procedures for installation of the new FCC software.
context: FAA statement that FAA approval of Boeing's proposed fixes and service bulletins constitutes proof they work and are appropriate.

label: TAB independently reviewed Boeing corrective actions
original_label: TAB independently reviewed Boeing corrective actions
quote: The FAA also commissioned a Technical Advisory Board (TAB) to independently review Boeing's proposed corrective actions. The TAB consisted of a number of technical experts with no involvement in the initial certification of the 737 MAX. Several of these experts were from other U.S. government agencies. The actions by the FAA and Boeing, summarized in this report, adopted the TAB's recommendations.
context: FAA description of how independent experts reviewed Boeing's fixes, implying that independent validation absolves FAA of responsibility for the original certification.

label: MCAS maximum command limit ensures pilot control
original_label: MCAS maximum command limit ensures pilot control
quote: This change limits the total amount of airplane nose-down stabilizer movement MCAS can command if there are repeated MCAS activations. This ensures that the flightcrew will always have maneuver capability through control column inputs alone, enabling the flightcrew to maintain level flight without requiring use of the electric trim switches or the stabilizer trim cutout switches.
context: FAA and Boeing characterization of the MCAS command limit as ensuring safety, despite fact that the original design lacked this protection and caused two fatal accidents.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: System meets all regulatory requirements for control force feel
original_label: System meets all regulatory requirements for control force feel
quote: These are not areas of the flight envelope in which the airplane normally operates. However, FAA regulations - specifically 14 CFR 25.143, 25.201, 25.203, 25.251, and 25.255 - still require the control column to have a higher pull-force feel in these flight regimes than would exist on the 737 MAX without the added stability from the STS and MCAS function.
context: FAA explanation of why MCAS was necessary, framed as regulatory compliance rather than a design choice with risks.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: No STS failure modes rely on pilot action alone
original_label: No STS failure modes rely on pilot action alone
quote: The FAA's review of the integrated SSA included an evaluation of Boeing's STS design changes to determine if any STS failure modes rely on pilot reaction times to maintain safe operation of the aircraft. The FAA's review of the integrated SSA and validated through extensive failure modes testing in simulators, the FAA concluded that no STS failure modes rely on exceptional piloting skills, and do not rely on immediate pilot actions.
context: FAA conclusion that the redesigned system does not depend on pilot response, reducing accountability for those who must operate it.

label: Critics unqualified to make hazard judgments
original_label: Critics unqualified to make hazard judgments
quote: The TAB provided a commentary on certification considerations that suggests, as a routine matter for any certification project, the proposed CB pull NNCs should be supported by the necessary certification data. Ergonomic data and simulator test data need to be evaluated for compliance with all applicable regulations. In consideration of the TAB's opinion, the FAA and Boeing considered an alternative Airspeed Unreliable NNC that includes the use of a circuit breaker to disable an erroneous stick shaker on the 737 MAX aircraft. The FAA evaluated this alternative NNC in addition to the same NNC (without a circuit breaker pull) used in our certification testing of 737 MAX post-accident design changes. The FAA evaluation used multiple crews that included three certification-flight test pilots and three operations evaluation pilots who were all 737 type rated with a broad range of operational experience.
context: FAA and Boeing response to criticism about circuit breaker accessibility, asserting their evaluation methods and pilot credentials as superior to critics'.

label: FAA testing showed international critics wrong
original_label: FAA testing showed international critics wrong
quote: The FAA's test results found that all participants agreed that the alternative NNC (with CB pull) may not be in alignment with the intent of 14 CFR 25.777(a) and (c). Although the crews were eventually able to reach and successfully pull the appropriate circuit breaker, they were not able to do so while seated with their seat belt and shoulder harness properly fastened, or without excessively deviating their attention from their primary duties of pilot flying or pilot monitoring.
context: FAA presentation of its own testing as definitive proof that international authority suggestions were unsafe, dismissing their expertise.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Erroneous high-AOA event is major not hazardous
original_label: Erroneous high-AOA event is major not hazardous
quote: The FAA essentially answered this fundamental question as 'no' by concluding that the effect on the airplane and crew of the failure is 'Major' in the context of § 25.1309 System Safety Analysis and associated Functional Hazard Assessment. That is, safety margins are reduced, and crew workload is increased, however the failure does not excessively impair the crew's ability to perform their duties. In accordance with FAA regulations and policy, and considering the probability and testing of failure effects if the effect is 'Major', the airplane can still be operated safely, so using the FAA determination a false stick-shaker activation does not need to be suppressed.
context: FAA use of regulatory classification (Major vs. Hazardous) to justify rejecting calls for additional safety measures, treating technical categorization as settling moral question.

label: Each State of Registry responsible for airworthiness
original_label: Each State of Registry responsible for airworthiness
quote: Each State of Registry is responsible for the continued airworthiness and continued operational safety (COS) of aircraft on its registry. Accordingly, all States of Registry should adopt the final FAA AD and mandate the same changes in their own systems.
context: FAA statement allocating responsibility to other national regulators rather than retaining oversight of its own design approval.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: FAA commitment to transparency and continuous improvement
original_label: FAA commitment to transparency and continuous improvement
quote: The FAA has a longstanding commitment to transparency, continuous improvement, and information sharing to encourage increased aviation safety worldwide. To these ends, the agency supported numerous reviews, investigations, and robust international engagement with fellow Civil Aviation Authorities (CAAs).
context: FAA appeal to its institutional mission and values to justify its handling of the 737 MAX certification and return to service.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Software development assurance meets FAA and EASA standards
original_label: Software development assurance meets FAA and EASA standards
quote: Boeing demonstrated compliance with software development assurance (DA) requirements for the 737 MAX Enhanced Digital Flight Control System (EDFCS) in accordance with FAA and European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) processes. The software DA process defines how Boeing develops, validates, verifies and manages software functional requirements.
context: FAA statement that compliance with DA processes and standards constitutes adequate proof that software is safe.

label: Multiple MCAS activations no longer expected to occur
original_label: Multiple MCAS activations no longer expected to occur
quote: Due to the MCAS changes previously discussed, this command limit is not expected to be used but provides an additional level of safety.
context: FAA characterization of a safety feature as an extra layer not expected to be needed, downplaying the risk it was designed to prevent.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: MCAS activation thresholds retained for nominal conditions
original_label: MCAS activation thresholds retained for nominal conditions
quote: The updated MCAS design retains the original MCAS activation thresholds for nominal conditions (i.e., absent sensor failures or pilot electric trim interaction).
context: FAA statement that the original MCAS design parameters were retained, treating this as evidence of appropriateness rather than concern.

label: Boeing responsible for showing compliance demonstrations
original_label: Boeing responsible for showing compliance demonstrations
quote: The applicant describes the proposed change to the FAA, and includes functional and design details pertinent to the certification project. The applicant prepares a certification plan using requirements established by that model's certification basis at the time of type certification (or amended type certification for a derivative such as the 737 MAX), as well as a description of how it will show compliance, including any airplane test activities.
context: FAA description of certification process where manufacturer bears responsibility for developing compliance evidence.

label: Stabilizer movement described as incremental commands
original_label: Stabilizer movement described as incremental commands
quote: In the original design, all MCAS commands were incremental commands, which moved the horizontal stabilizer a fixed amount, regardless of the current position of the stabilizer.
context: FAA characterization of repetitive nose-down trim inputs that pilots could not counter as neutral technical 'incremental commands'.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: MCAS necessary to comply with control force regulations
original_label: MCAS necessary to comply with control force regulations
quote: For the FAA to certify the 737 MAX, the original design had to meet FAA requirements for control force feel when maneuvering or deviating significantly from trimmed equilibrium. The aircraft manufacturer is responsible for making design decisions and showing compliance to applicable regulations. In this case, Boeing elected to include an additional flight control law in the STS, which is part of the flight control software that provides required control force feel to the pilot.
context: FAA explanation that regulatory compliance necessitated MCAS inclusion, framing it as mandatory rather than discretionary design choice.

label: AOA sensor failures not detected by ADIRU systems
original_label: AOA sensor failures not detected by ADIRU systems
quote: Certain AOA sensor failures are not related to degradation of the electrical circuit, and therefore are not detected by the ADIRU. These failures result in AOA values transmitted by the ADIRU as 'valid' when, in fact, they are not correct. These outputs of the ADIRU are referred to as 'valid erroneous' data. Examples of failures that result in erroneous data include a bent or broken AOA vane (e.g. due to a bird strike or ramp damage) or a mis-calibrated AOA sensor (e.g. JT610 scenario).
context: FAA technical description of sensor failure modes that appeared in the accident, presented matter-of-factly without emphasizing the system's vulnerability.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Split vane monitor threshold meets design standards
original_label: Split vane monitor threshold meets design standards
quote: The AOA split-vane monitor threshold is large enough to allow for expected variations in AOA sensors but small enough to prevent MCAS activation due to erroneous AOA data.
context: FAA statement that the threshold meets engineering design principles, treating this as settling whether it adequately protects against sensor failures.

label: Effect on pilot recognition is not hazardous but major
original_label: Effect on pilot recognition is not hazardous but major
quote: That is, safety margins are reduced, and crew workload is increased, however the failure does not excessively impair the crew's ability to perform their duties.
context: FAA regulatory characterization minimizing the consequences of an erroneous high-AOA event that killed 346 people in two accidents.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Certification requirements have been retained
original_label: Certification requirements have been retained
quote: Certification requirements are the regulations applicable to the systems and functions that are changed, as well as the airplane-level compliance effects of those changes. The amendment levels of the regulations are determined at the time of Amended Type Certification, as captured in the Certification Basis in the FAA Type Certification Data Sheet (TCDS) A16WE.
context: FAA technical statement treating the retention of certification requirements as adequate proof of design safety.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Pilot action assumptions challenged but not disowned
original_label: Pilot action assumptions challenged but not disowned
quote: During the original certification of the 737 MAX and again after the accidents, the FAA required Boeing to assess potential failures of the flight control system, as well as potential flightcrew responses to those failures. The FAA evaluated Boeing's assessment of flightcrew alerting and found that it complies with regulatory requirements.
context: FAA statement that it required and reviewed Boeing's pilot response assumptions, but accepts Boeing's compliance assessment rather than independently validating assumptions.

label: International suggestions introduce new safety hazards
original_label: International suggestions introduce new safety hazards
quote: One evaluator had to exit his seat and required an extended period of time to locate the circuit breaker. The FAA further found that the participants questioned the system meeting several other regulations (§§ 25.771, 25.1301, 25.1309, 25.1585). The FAA considered potential cases where a pilot pulled a nearby but incorrect circuit breaker. In one case, pulling the wrong circuit breaker indeed silenced the erroneous stick shaker but introduced other flight-deck effects that produced new and undetected hazards.
context: FAA testing and presentation of international CAA suggestions as creating new hazards, dismissing them as unsafe.

label: Each CAA makes its own assessment and validation
original_label: Each CAA makes its own assessment and validation
quote: Each authority will make its own assessment of the FAA's process and findings, as well as Boeing's actions to address the findings. Due to the nature of the certification process, the FAA continually engaged with the CAAs on all aspects of the review. Likewise, all of the CAAs reviewed identical data from Boeing to make their respective findings.
context: FAA statement allocating decision-making to other CAAs rather than retaining central responsibility for safety of the original certification.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Changes comply with entire certification basis
original_label: Changes comply with entire certification basis
quote: The FAA reviewed and cross referenced systems without relying on Boeing's computer-aided design tools. The integrated SSA enabled the FAA to trace systems and make safety determinations using a single document that integrated the analysis, rather than simultaneous tracing through multiple documents. Reliance on Pilot Mitigations The FAA's review of the integrated SSA included an evaluation of Boeing's STS design changes to determine if any STS failure modes rely on pilot reaction times to maintain safe operation of the aircraft.
context: FAA statement about its review methods and conclusions that no STS failures rely on pilot reaction times, treated as proof that design is safe.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Transparency and information sharing promote aviation safety
original_label: Transparency and information sharing promote aviation safety
quote: The FAA has a longstanding commitment to transparency, continuous improvement and a global exchange of safety-related information that encourages increased aviation safety worldwide.
context: FAA appeal to its institutional commitment to transparency and safety as foundation for its actions on 737 MAX.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: State of Design obligation to provide safety information
original_label: State of Design obligation to provide safety information
quote: The U.S., as the State of Design for the 737 MAX and signatory on the Convention on International Civil Aviation (Chicago Convention), is obliged to provide all States of Registry for the 737 MAX with the safety information they need to oversee the safe operation of the aircraft within their national systems.
context: FAA appeal to international legal obligations and conventions to justify its role and decisions.

label: MCAS activation and resynchronization logic limits commands
original_label: MCAS activation and resynchronization logic limits commands
quote: The updated MCAS design retains the original MCAS activation thresholds for nominal conditions (i.e., absent sensor failures or pilot electric trim interaction). The revised MCAS activation criteria now include a requirement for the AOA to transition from a low AOA state (below the threshold) to a high AOA state (above the threshold) after the airplane is in the configuration and flight region where MCAS is utilized (flaps up and manual flight). This single activation of MCAS will be limited to maximum of 2.5 degrees of airplane nose-down stabilizer motion (which is referred to as a single MCAS command).
context: FAA and Boeing characterization of the revised MCAS design as limiting commands, minimizing the significance of original unlimited repetitive activation.

label: Speed trim system inoperative rendered as maintenance item
original_label: Speed trim system inoperative rendered as maintenance item
quote: When MCAS and Speed Trim are disabled, SPEED TRIM FAIL is annunciated and a maintenance item is recorded.
context: Technical characterization of loss of critical stabilizer functions as a routine maintenance record item, using sanitized language.

label: Crew actions inconsistent with manufacturer assumptions
original_label: Crew actions inconsistent with manufacturer assumptions
quote: During the accident flight, the system malfunction led to erroneous information that initiated a series of events that were not correctly recognized and responded to by the flightcrew. This exposed issues that were not identified if Federal Aviation Regulation (FAR) 25.1302 and 25.1309 were each considered separately.
context: KNKT recommendation as quoted by FAA, framing the problem as crew recognition failures and regulatory gaps rather than design failure.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Design change demonstrates compliance with all regulations
original_label: Design change demonstrates compliance with all regulations
quote: The FAA has determined that Boeing's proposed changes to the 737 MAX design, flightcrew procedures and maintenance procedures effectively mitigate the airplane-related safety issues that contributed to the Flight 610 and Flight 302 accidents. The FAA further determined that the proposed design change also address safety concerns beyond those that the accident investigations identified.
context: FAA statement that its determination of regulatory compliance constitutes assurance that design changes are effective and safe.

label: FAA support for multiple independent reviews and investigations
original_label: FAA support for multiple independent reviews and investigations
quote: The FAA and other U.S. bodies commissioned a number of studies to evaluate the initial certification of the 737 MAX, as well as the certification process itself. The FAA invited nine other CAAs to be a part of the Joint Authorities Technical Review (JATR), which assessed the certification of the 737 MAX flight control system.
context: FAA statement about commissioning independent reviews, implying that delegation of evaluation absolves FAA of responsibility.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Individual defendants deny personal knowledge of misbranding
original_label: Individual defendants deny personal knowledge of misbranding
quote: The individual defendants are not charged with personal knowledge of the misbranding or with any personal intent to defraud.
context: The court describes the charges against the three individual executives (Friedman, Udell, and Goldenheim) in the plea agreement.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: Individual defendants agree to facts without admitting knowledge
original_label: Individual defendants agree to facts without admitting knowledge
quote: Purdue has agreed that these facts are true, and the individual defendants, while they do not agree that they had knowledge of these things, have agreed that the court may accept these facts in support of their guilty pleas.
context: The court describes how the defendants entered their pleas while denying personal awareness of the conduct.

label: Purdue relies on legal advice to limit restitution
original_label: Purdue relies on legal advice to limit restitution
quote: The government and the defendants, in agreeing to preclude other restitution, rely on the Victim and Witness Protection Act of 1982 (VWPA), which states in relevant part as follows: To the extent that the court determines that the complication and prolongation of the sentencing process resulting from the fashioning of an order of restitution under this section outweighs the need to provide restitution to any victims, the court may decline to make such an order.
context: The defendants justify excluding restitution to private victims by invoking statutory language and legal authority.

label: Purdue defers drug policy to federal agencies
original_label: Purdue defers drug policy to federal agencies
quote: The government has represented that it did not demand inclusion of a treatment provision in the plea agreements because national drug policy has been placed by Congress in the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Service Administration, an agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. The government prosecutors were reluctant to direct treatment funds in a manner beyond their expertise and possibly contrary to national policy.
context: The government and defendants explain why the plea agreement contains no allocation for drug treatment or education, citing delegation of policy authority to other agencies.

label: Causation barriers minimize individual victim harm
original_label: Causation barriers minimize individual victim harm
quote: Courts have consistently found that despite extensive discovery, plaintiffs were unable to show that Purdue's misbranding proximately caused their injuries. See, e.g., Bodie v. Purdue Pharma Co., No. 05-13834, 2007 WL 1577964, at *3 (11th Cir. June 1, 2007) (affirming the district court's conclusion that the plaintiff's claims failed because he could not show that he was proximately harmed by Purdue's allegedly inadequate warnings); Koenig v. Purdue Pharma Co., 435 F. Supp. 2d 551, 556 (N.D. Tex. 2006) (Because plaintiffs have failed to show that an adequate warning would have changed [the physician]'s decision to prescribe OxyContin, and because [the physician] testified that he would not have changed his decision, the Court finds that Plaintiffs have failed to raise a genuine fact issue.).
context: The court documents legal precedent showing that individual injury victims could not prove causation between Purdue's misbranding and their harm, effectively diminishing their standing as victims.

label: Chain of causation broken by intervening conduct
original_label: Chain of causation broken by intervening conduct
quote: Purdue further argues that the chain of causation between the harm alleged and the misbranding offense could have been broken by any intervening act on behalf of the insured patient or the prescribing health care professional. For example, if patients obtained OxyContin improperly by deceiving their physicians or by altering an otherwise proper prescription, the third-party payors would not be entitled to restitution for those prescriptions since the misbranding did not directly and proximately caused any financial loss to the third-party payor. Or if a physician negligently prescribed OxyContin, the third-party payor that paid for that prescription is also not entitled to restitution because the misbranding once again did not directly and proximately cause the third-party payor's financial loss.
context: Purdue's argument presented to the court to minimize liability by attributing harm to intervening actions of patients or physicians rather than to the company's misbranding.

label: Defendants cite civic commitment and positive attributes
original_label: Defendants cite civic commitment and positive attributes
quote: The defendants point to their lack of prior criminal record, their strong commitment to civic and charitable endeavors, as well as their other positive personal attributes.
context: The defendants' counsel present their prior good conduct and charitable work as mitigating factors against criminal sanctions.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: OxyContin marketed for pain relief broader applications
original_label: OxyContin marketed for pain relief broader applications
quote: Because of the addictive quality of opioids, doctors had traditionally reserved their use for cancer patients and those "with chronic diseases." But OxyContin, Purdue claimed, had a novel "time-release" formula that greatly diminished the threat of addiction. On that basis, Purdue marketed OxyContin for use in "a much broader range" of applications, including as a "first-line therapy for the treatment of arthritis."
context: Majority opinion's recitation of Purdue's marketing rationale in the factual background, presenting Purdue's claimed purpose of pain management.

label: Sacklers seek judicial order to bind victims
original_label: Sacklers seek judicial order to bind victims
quote: the Sacklers wanted to extinguish any claims the estate might have against family members, including for fraudulently transferring funds from Purdue in the years preceding its bankruptcy. Second, the Sacklers wanted to end the growing number of lawsuits against them brought by opioid victims (the Sackler discharge). The Sackler discharge they proposed comprised a release and an injunction.
context: Majority opinion describing how Sacklers shifted their responsibility through a court order rather than their own bankruptcy filing.

label: Bankruptcy Court found settlement was fair given collection difficulties
original_label: Bankruptcy Court found settlement was fair given collection difficulties
quote: Indeed, after a 6-day trial involving 41 witnesses, the Bankruptcy Court found that the settlement provided the best chance for the victims and creditors to ever see any money from the Sacklers. The Bankruptcy Court found that the creditors' and victims' ability to recover directly from any of the Sacklers in tort litigation was far from certain. Even if the suits were successful, the Bankruptcy Court expressed "significant concern" about the ability to collect any judgments from the Sacklers due to the difficulty of reaching their assets in foreign countries and in spendthrift trusts.
context: Dissent (Justice Kavanaugh) recounting the Bankruptcy Court's factual findings to minimize the harm of accepting a lower settlement amount.

label: Sacklers' settlement payment offsets liability
original_label: Sacklers' settlement payment offsets liability
quote: Standing alone, Purdue's estate is estimated to be worth approximately $1.8 billion—a small fraction of the sizable claims against Purdue. If that were all the money on the table, the Bankruptcy Court found, the victims and creditors "would probably recover nothing" from Purdue's estate. That is because the United States holds a $2 billion "superpriority" claim, meaning that the United States would be first in line to recover ahead of all of the victims and other creditors. The United States' claim would wipe out Purdue's entire $1.8 billion value. So for the victims and other creditors to have any hope of meaningful recovery, Purdue's bankruptcy estate needed more funds. Where to find those funds? The Sacklers' assets were the answer. After vigorous negotiations, a settlement was reached: In exchange for the releases, the Sacklers ultimately agreed to make significant payments to Purdue's estate—between $5.5 and $6 billion.
context: Dissent presenting the Sacklers' settlement payment as offsetting their liability and enabling victim recovery.

label: Victims would race to courthouse for selfish gain
original_label: Victims would race to courthouse for selfish gain
quote: By eliminating nonconsensual non-debtor releases, today's decision gives every victim and every creditor an absolute right to sue the Sacklers. Some may hold out from any potential future settlement and instead sue because they want to have their day in court to hold the defendants accountable, or because they want to try to hit the jackpot of a large recovery that they can keep all to themselves. Moreover, because every victim and creditor knows that the Sacklers' resources are limited, they will now have an incentive to promptly sue the Sacklers before others sue.
context: Dissent characterizing victims' behavior as self-interested holdout and race-to-courthouse behavior rather than legitimate pursuit of justice.

label: U.S. Trustee thwarting victims' interests
original_label: U.S. Trustee thwarting victims' interests
quote: The regional United States Trustee for three States, a Government bankruptcy watchdog appointed to oversee bankruptcy cases in those States, also opposes the plan for reasons that remain mystifying. The U. S. Trustee purports to look out for victims and creditors, but here the victims and creditors made emphatically clear that the "U. S. Trustee does not speak for the victims of the opioid crisis" and is indeed thwarting the opioid victims' efforts at fair and equitable recovery.
context: Dissent attacking the motives and legitimacy of the U.S. Trustee as a critic, claiming it does not represent victims' actual interests.

label: Court animated by hostility to Sacklers rather than law
original_label: Court animated by hostility to Sacklers rather than law
quote: To be sure, many Americans have deep hostility toward the Sacklers. But allowing that animosity to infect this bankruptcy case is entirely misdirected and counterproductive, and just piles even more injury onto the opioid victims.
context: Dissent suggesting the majority is driven by emotional hostility to Sacklers rather than legal reasoning.

label: Plan provides substantial compensation ranging $3,500 to $48,000
original_label: Plan provides substantial compensation ranging $3,500 to $48,000
quote: As for individual victims harmed by the company's products, Purdue offered, with help from the Sacklers' anticipated contribution, to provide payments from a base amount of $3,500 up to a ceiling of $48,000 (for the most dire cases, and all before deductions for attorney's fees and other expenses).
context: Majority opinion describing victim compensation amounts without emphasizing they require deductions and extend over many years.

label: Congress should decide opioid bankruptcy policy
original_label: Congress should decide opioid bankruptcy policy
quote: Someday, Congress may choose to add to the bankruptcy code special rules for opioid-related bankruptcies as it has for asbestos-related cases. Or it may choose not to do so. Either way, if a policy decision like that is to be made, it is for Congress to make.
context: Majority opinion deflecting responsibility for bankruptcy policy to Congress rather than courts.

label: Non-debtor releases in prior mass-tort bankruptcies solved important problems
original_label: Non-debtor releases in prior mass-tort bankruptcies solved important problems
quote: For decades, bankruptcy courts and courts of appeals have determined that non-debtor releases can be appropriate and essential in mass-tort cases like this one. Non-debtor releases have enabled substantial and equitable relief to victims in cases ranging from asbestos, Dalkon Shield, and Dow Corning silicone breast implants to the Catholic Church and the Boy Scouts.
context: Dissent using historical success of non-debtor releases in other cases to justify their use here.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: 2007 guilty plea to misbranding charges
original_label: 2007 guilty plea to misbranding charges
quote: In 2007, a Purdue affiliate pleaded guilty to a federal felony for misbranding OxyContin as "less addictive" and "less subject to abuse . . . than other pain medications."
context: Majority opinion citing formal legal admission of wrongdoing but not using it as a defense.

label: Sacklers initiated milking program
original_label: Sacklers initiated milking program
quote: Appreciating this litigation "would eventually impact them directly," the Sacklers began what one family member described as a "milking" program. In the years before the 2007 plea agreement, Purdue's distributions to the Sacklers represented less than 15% of its annual revenue. After the plea agreement, the Sacklers began taking as much as 70% of the company's revenue each year. Between 2008 and 2016, the family's distributions totaled approximately $11 billion, draining Purdue's total assets by 75% and leaving it in "a significantly weakened financial" state.
context: Majority opinion quoting a Sackler family member's own label for their asset-stripping behavior.

label: Plan quadrupled estate and enabled 95 percent creditor approval
original_label: Plan quadrupled estate and enabled 95 percent creditor approval
quote: Adding that substantial amount to Purdue's comparatively smaller bankruptcy estate enabled Purdue's reorganization plan to distribute an estimated $7 billion or more to the victims and creditors—thereby quadrupling the size of the estate available for distribution. With that enhanced estate, the plan garnered 95 percent support from the voting victims and creditors. That high level of support tends to show that this was a very good plan for the victims and creditors.
context: Dissent using high creditor vote percentage and estate enlargement to minimize the harm of non-consensual releases.

label: First successful plaintiffs would deplete assets for others
original_label: First successful plaintiffs would deplete assets for others
quote: One possibility is that no lawsuits against the Sacklers would succeed, and no victim or creditor would recover any money from them. And without the $5.5 to $6 billion settlement payment, there would be no recovery from Purdue either. Another possibility is that a large claim or claims would succeed, and the Sacklers would be indemnified by Purdue—thereby wiping out Purdue's estate for all of the other victims and creditors. Last, suppose that a large claim succeeded and that the Sacklers were not indemnified for that liability. Even in that case, only a few victims or creditors would be able to recover from the Sacklers at the expense of fair and equitable distribution to the rest of the victims and creditors.
context: Dissent portraying victims as inherently selfish actors who would deprive each other rather than cooperate fairly.

label: Non-debtor releases essential across multiple mass-tort contexts
original_label: Non-debtor releases essential across multiple mass-tort contexts
quote: Without a coordinating mechanism, a victim's (or group of victims') recovery against one local entity could have eaten up all of the shared insurance assets, leaving all of the other victims with nothing. Bankruptcy provided a forum to coordinate liability and insurance assets. A non-debtor release provision prevented victims from litigating outside of the bankruptcy plan's procedures. And the provision therefore prevented one victim or group of victims from obtaining all of the insurance funds before other victims recovered.
context: Dissent comparing non-debtor releases favorably to uncoordinated tort litigation outcomes in Boy Scouts and Catholic Church bankruptcies.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Bankruptcy system designed to ensure fair and equitable recovery
original_label: Bankruptcy system designed to ensure fair and equitable recovery
quote: The bankruptcy system is designed to preserve the debtor's estate so as to ensure fair and equitable recovery for creditors. Bankruptcy courts achieve that overarching objective by, among other things, releasing claims that otherwise could deplete the estate for the benefit of only a few and leave all the other creditors with nothing.
context: Dissent justifying non-debtor releases by appeal to bankruptcy law's higher purpose of fair and equitable victim recovery.

label: Parties negotiated and settled on release terms
original_label: Parties negotiated and settled on release terms
quote: After vigorous negotiations, a settlement was reached: In exchange for the releases, the Sacklers ultimately agreed to make significant payments to Purdue's estate—between $5.5 and $6 billion. That settlement—exchanging releases for the Sacklers' $5.5 to $6 billion payment—enabled the victims and creditors to avoid "the significant risk, cost and delay (potentially years) that would result from pursuing the Sacklers and related parties through litigation."
context: Dissent describing the releases as part of a negotiated settlement rather than imposed terms.

label: Non-debtor releases described as traditional litigation settlement
original_label: Non-debtor releases described as traditional litigation settlement
quote: As courts have always recognized, non-debtor releases are different. Non-debtor releases "do not offer the umbrella protection of a discharge in bankruptcy." Rather, non-debtor releases are accompanied by settlement payments to the estate by the non-debtor. So non-debtor releases are simply one part of a settlement of pending or potential claims against the non-debtor that arise out of some torts committed by the debtor. They are in essence a traditional litigation settlement.
context: Dissent using technical distinction and traditional terminology to normalize non-debtor releases.

label: Court second-guessing settlement amount without factual basis
original_label: Court second-guessing settlement amount without factual basis
quote: To begin with, even if that were true, it would not be a reason to categorically disallow non-debtor releases as a matter of law, as the Court does today. In any event, that concern is unsupported by the record and contradicted by the Bankruptcy Court's undisputed findings of fact. The Bankruptcy Court found that the creditors' and victims' ability to recover directly from any of the Sacklers in tort litigation was far from certain. The Court today has no good basis for its subtle second-guessing of the settlement amount.
context: Dissent attacking the majority for questioning the settlement amount contrary to the factual record.

label: Victims and creditors desperately need the plan
original_label: Victims and creditors desperately need the plan
quote: Without the releases, there will be no $5.5 to $6 billion settlement payment to the estate, and "there will be no viable path to any victim recovery." Tr. of Oral Arg. 100. And without the plan's substantial funding to prevent and treat opioid addiction, the victims and creditors bluntly described further repercussions: "more people will die without this Plan."
context: Dissent minimizing the harm of eliminating non-debtor releases by emphasizing victims' dependence on the plan.

label: Victims characterized as uninformed about their own interests
original_label: Victims characterized as uninformed about their own interests
quote: And it is rather paternalistic for the Court to tell the victims that they should have done better—and then to turn around and leave them with potentially nothing.
context: Dissent attacking the majority for disregarding victims' own expressed preferences about settlement.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Plan provisions narrowly tailored to legal requirement
original_label: Plan provisions narrowly tailored to legal requirement
quote: The non-debtor releases of claims against the Sacklers prevented that collective-action problem in the same way that the releases of claims against Purdue itself prevented the identical collective-action problem. Both protected Purdue's assets from being consumed by the first to sue successfully. And the non-debtor releases were narrowly tailored to the problem. The non-debtor releases enjoined victims and creditors from bringing claims against the Sacklers only in cases where Purdue's conduct, or the victims' or creditors' claims asserted against Purdue, was a legal cause or a legally relevant factor to the cause of action against the Sacklers.
context: Dissent justifying non-debtor releases as meeting technical legal requirements of narrow tailoring.

label: Settlement amount reflected realistic probability of recovery
original_label: Settlement amount reflected realistic probability of recovery
quote: From the victims' and creditors' perspective, "suing the Sacklers would have been a costly endeavor with a small chance of success. From the Sacklers' perspective, defending those suits would have been a costly endeavor with a very small chance of a large liability." So as in many litigation settlements, the parties agreed to the $5.5 to $6 billion settlement in light of that "very small chance of a large liability."
context: Dissent minimizing the Sacklers' payments by characterizing them as reasonable settlement compensation given litigation uncertainty.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Bankruptcy court served fair and equitable victim compensation
original_label: Bankruptcy court served fair and equitable victim compensation
quote: The bankruptcy system works to preserve a bankrupt company's limited assets and to then fairly and equitably distribute those assets among the creditors—and in mass-tort bankruptcies, among the victims.
context: Dissent opening by stating bankruptcy's higher purpose of fair distribution to justify non-debtor releases.

label: Court throws out plan based on animosity to Sacklers
original_label: Court throws out plan based on animosity to Sacklers
quote: But the Court now throws out the plan—and in doing so, categorically prohibits non-debtor releases, which have long been a critical tool for bankruptcy courts to manage mass-tort bankruptcies like this one. That is true, the Court says, even when (as here) those non-debtor releases are necessary to facilitate a fair settlement with the officers and directors and produce a significantly larger bankruptcy estate that can be fairly and equitably distributed among the victims and creditors.
context: Dissent criticizing the majority for applying a categorical rule motivated by hostility rather than legal reasoning.

label: Bankruptcy preferable to class action and multi-district litigation
original_label: Bankruptcy preferable to class action and multi-district litigation
quote: In many cases, there is no workable alternative other than bankruptcy for achieving fair and equitable recovery for mass-tort victims. "Outside of bankruptcy," victims face "significant administrative costs" of multi-district litigation, "which has limited coordination mechanisms and no tools for binding future claimants." And multi-district litigation cannot "solve the collective action problem because dissenting claimants can opt out of settlements even when super majorities favor them." Bankruptcy, on the other hand, reduces administrative costs and allows all of the affected parties to come together, pause litigation elsewhere, invoke procedural safeguards including discovery, and reach a collective resolution that considers both current and future victims.
context: Dissent comparing bankruptcy favorably to alternative dispute resolution mechanisms for mass torts.

label: Sacklers offered releases as condition of settlement payment
original_label: Sacklers offered releases as condition of settlement payment
quote: But they offered to do so only through payments spread out over a decade. And, in return, they sought the estate's agreement on, and a judicial order addressing, two matters. First, the Sacklers wanted to extinguish any claims the estate might have against family members, including for fraudulently transferring funds from Purdue in the years preceding its bankruptcy. Second, the Sacklers wanted to end the growing number of lawsuits against them brought by opioid victims (the Sackler discharge).
context: Majority describing how Sacklers made releases a condition of their settlement payment, thereby shifting burden to victims.

label: 50 state attorneys general signed on to plan
original_label: 50 state attorneys general signed on to plan
quote: Now, all 50 States have signed on to the plan. The lineup before this Court is telling. On one side of the case: the tens of thousands of opioid victims and their families; more than 4,000 state, city, county, tribal, and local government entities; and more than 40,000 hospitals and healthcare organizations. They all urge the Court to uphold the plan.
context: Dissent citing widespread political and institutional support as evidence of plan's legitimacy.

label: Without releases, victims face liquidation with no recovery
original_label: Without releases, victims face liquidation with no recovery
quote: Absent the releases and settlement payment, the Bankruptcy Court found, the "most likely result" would be liquidation of a much smaller $1.8 billion estate. In a liquidation, the United States would recover first with its $2 billion superpriority claim, taking for itself the whole pie. And the victims and other creditors "would probably recover nothing."
context: Dissent minimizing concerns about non-debtor releases by stressing devastating alternative outcome.

category: Diffusion of responsibility and denial of personal involvement
label: No party challenged appropriateness of releases in this case
original_label: No party challenged appropriateness of releases in this case
quote: Yet that is not the path the Court takes. The Court does not contest the Bankruptcy Court's and Second Circuit's conclusion that a non-debtor release was necessary and appropriate for the settlement and the success of Purdue's reorganization—the best, and perhaps the only, chance for victims and creditors to receive fair and equitable compensation. Indeed, no party has challenged the Bankruptcy Court's factual findings or made an argument that non-debtor releases were used inappropriately in this specific case.
context: Dissent noting that even opposing parties did not challenge the releases' appropriateness in this case.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Sacklers' settlement payment was properly negotiated settlement
original_label: Sacklers' settlement payment was properly negotiated settlement
quote: The settlement amount of $5.5 to $6 billion was "properly negotiated" and "reflects the underlying strengths and weaknesses of the opposing parties' legal positions and issues of collection."
context: Dissent citing Bankruptcy Court finding that settlement reflected proper negotiation process and legal analysis.

label: Releases described as solving collective action problems
original_label: Releases described as solving collective action problems
quote: The non-debtor release provision prevented a race to the courthouse against the Sacklers. As a result, the non-debtor release provision solved two separate collective-action problems that dogged Purdue's mass-tort bankruptcy: (i) It protected Purdue's estate from the risk of being depleted by indemnification claims, and (ii) it operated as a settlement of potential claims against the Sacklers and thus enabled the Sacklers' large settlement payment to the estate.
context: Dissent using technical economic language to normalize contested release provisions.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Plan solved complex collective action problems among victims
original_label: Plan solved complex collective action problems among victims
quote: Mass-tort cases present the same collective-action problem that bankruptcy was designed to address. "Without a mandatory rule that consolidates claims in a single tribunal, tort claimants would rationally enter a race to the courthouse." The "plaintiffs who bring successful suits earlier are likely to drain the firm's resources, while inconsistent judgments could result in inequitable payouts even among plaintiffs who ultimately do collect."
context: Dissent justifying releases by appeal to bankruptcy's foundational purpose of preventing destructive competition among creditors.

label: Victimization would continue and multiply without plan
original_label: Victimization would continue and multiply without plan
quote: more people will die without this Plan
context: Dissent quoting victims and creditors' characterization that plan rejection will cause further deaths.

label: Court prioritizes punishment over victim compensation
original_label: Court prioritizes punishment over victim compensation
quote: Nothing is more antithetical to the purpose of bankruptcy than destroying estate value to punish someone.
context: Dissent accusing majority of allowing hostility to Sacklers to override bankruptcy's compensation purpose.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Non-debtor releases confined to narrow factually-defined circumstances
original_label: Non-debtor releases confined to narrow factually-defined circumstances
quote: Historical and contemporary practice demonstrate that non-debtor releases are especially appropriate when (as here) non-debtor releases and corresponding settlement payments preserve and increase the debtor's estate and thereby ensure fair and equitable recovery for creditors. Over those decades of practice, courts have developed and applied numerous factors for determining whether a non-debtor release is "appropriate" in a given case. Those factors reflect the fact that determining whether a non-debtor release is "appropriate" is a holistic inquiry that depends on the precise facts and circumstances of each case. And the factors have served to confine the use of non-debtor releases to well-defined and narrow circumstances—precisely those circumstances where the collective-action problems arise.
context: Dissent arguing non-debtor releases satisfy technical legal requirements developed over decades of practice.

label: Indemnified officers' liability characterized as estate liability
original_label: Indemnified officers' liability characterized as estate liability
quote: In such cases, "a suit against the non-debtor is, in essence, a suit against the debtor." If not barred from doing so, the creditors could race to the courthouse against the indemnified officers and directors for basically the same claims that they hold against the debtor company. If successful, such suits would deplete the company's assets because a judgment against the indemnified officers and directors would likely come out of the debtor company's assets.
context: Dissent using "in essence" language to elide distinction between debtor and indemnified non-debtor releases.

label: Alternative mechanisms cannot solve mass-tort coordination
original_label: Alternative mechanisms cannot solve mass-tort coordination
quote: bankruptcy "provides the only forum in the U. S. legal system where a unified and complete resolution of mass-tort cases can reliably occur in a manner that results in a fair recovery and distribution for all claimants." And the bankruptcy system could not do so without non-debtor releases.
context: Dissent comparing bankruptcy favorably to other legal forums as uniquely capable of fair mass-tort resolution.

label: Victims reduced to strategic actors pursuing self-interest
original_label: Victims reduced to strategic actors pursuing self-interest
quote: Some may hold out from any potential future settlement and instead sue because they want to have their day in court to hold the defendants accountable, or because they want to try to hit the jackpot of a large recovery that they can keep all to themselves.
context: Dissent portraying victims' litigation rights as motivated by vengeance and greed rather than justice.

label: Bankruptcy court and Second Circuit appropriately approved releases
original_label: Bankruptcy court and Second Circuit appropriately approved releases
quote: the Bankruptcy Court and Second Circuit concluded that the non-debtor releases here not only were appropriate, but were essential to the success of the plan. The Bankruptcy Court and Second Circuit thoroughly analyzed each of the relevant factors before reaching that conclusion
context: Dissent diffusing responsibility for the releases to lower courts' reasoned judgment.

category: Moral justification and appeal to higher loyalties
label: Plan preserved estate and ensured equitable victim distribution
original_label: Plan preserved estate and ensured equitable victim distribution
quote: Both sets of releases were necessary to preserve Purdue's estate so that it was available for all victims and creditors to recover fairly and equitably. Otherwise, the estate could be zeroed out: A few victims or creditors could race to the courthouse and obtain recovery from Purdue or the Sacklers (ultimately the same pot of money) and thereby deplete the assets of the company and leave nothing for everyone else.
context: Dissent justifying releases by appeal to fairness and equitable treatment among all victims.

label: Non-debtor releases characterized as traditional tort settlement
original_label: Non-debtor releases characterized as traditional tort settlement
quote: They are in essence a traditional litigation settlement. They are not a blanket discharge for the non-debtor. Here, therefore, the releases apply only to certain claims against the Sacklers—namely, those "that arise out of or relate to" Purdue's bankruptcy.
context: Dissent normalizing contested non-debtor releases through conventional settlement terminology.

category: Appeal to legality and technical compliance
label: Vehicles certified to emissions standards
original_label: Vehicles certified to emissions standards
quote: All three test vehicles were compliant with EPA Tier2-Bin5, as well as California LEV-II ULEV (for Vehicles A and B) and LEV-II LEV (for Vehicle C) emissions standards as per EPA certification documents.
context: The report notes that all vehicles tested met regulatory certification standards, establishing their legal compliance baseline.

label: Vehicles passed malfunction checks
original_label: Vehicles passed malfunction checks
quote: Furthermore, all three test vehicles were thoroughly checked for possible engine or after-treatment malfunction codes using an ECU scanning tool prior to selecting a vehicle for this on-road measurement campaign, with none of them showing any fault code or other anomalies.
context: The testing facility asserts that vehicles had no diagnostic trouble codes, implying they were operating as designed and within normal parameters.

label: After-treatment assumed de-greened
original_label: After-treatment assumed de-greened
quote: The after-treatment system was assumed to be 'de-greened' as all three vehicles have accumulated more than 3,000 to 4,000 miles, and no reduction in catalytic activity due to aging was expected as the total mileage was relatively low (< 15,000 miles) for all test vehicles.
context: The researchers rationalize that the catalytic systems were fully activated and not degraded, despite evidence in the results showing significant NOx exceedances.

label: On-road NOx higher but chassis dyno compliant
original_label: On-road NOx higher but chassis dyno compliant
